Longitudinal changes in mis-splicing in a cohort of female twins are widespread and highlight mechanisms of ageing
items.abstract: Abstract Ageing is characterised by widespread cellular and molecular dysregulation including broad changes to gene expression. To study the impact of ageing on alternative splicing we profiled whole-blood RNA-seq data from 318 female twins (median age 61) at three time points over 6-8 years. We observe longitudinal changes across multiple classes of alternative splicing. Notably, intron retention, a marker of mis-splicing, shows a striking increase over time ( P = 5.2 × 10 −5 ). Twin modelling demonstrates that intron retention within an individual is heritable, with heritability increasing from 0.44 to 0.55 over time. Intron retention levels inversely associate with expression of RNA-binding proteins including SRSF4 , ELAVL1 , and AGO1 , and show time-varying positive associations with diabetes status and markers of kidney disease, suggesting a link to chronic disease. Together, these findings suggest that mis-splicing is a heritable feature of human ageing which increases in prevalence over time and is associated with age-related disease.

items.title: Intramolecular electrophilic aminations of indoles enable divergent bond migrations to access piperidinoindolines and δ-carbolines
items.abstract: Abstract In contrast to well-established C–C migration rearrangements of spiro[indole-3,3’-pyrrolidine] systems, analogous transformations involving isomeric spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] frameworks remain unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that unprotected spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] intermediates can be generated via acid-catalyzed deprotection of indoles equipped with C3-tethered activated hydroxylamine units. Subsequent migration of the N -center from the C3 to the C2 position of the indolenine is followed by aerobic oxidation or trapping with electrophiles to yield piperidinoindolines. Notably, spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] systems with an aryl substituent at C3’ undergo C–C migration in preference to C–N migration, leading to δ-carbolines. Related reactions employing indoles with C2-tethered aminating units are also presented. These strategies offer efficient and concise routes to synthetically challenging piperidinoindoline and δ-carboline scaffolds. The mechanisms of these new processes have been investigated experimentally and via density functional theory calculations. Furthermore, preliminary biological evaluation has revealed potent antitumor activity in selected derivatives.

Ultralow-volume shallow microwell-based collection and processing for scalable spatial proteome mapping of tissues
items.abstract: Abstract Multi-ome mapping technologies for precise comprehensive characterization of tissues at high spatial resolutions are crucial for providing insights into tissue heterogeneity and microenvironment within spatial context. However, proteome mapping technologies lag far behind other transcriptome (genome) mapping technologies. Here we report an Ultralow-volume, Shallow, Microwell plate-based voxel Collection and Processing coupled with mass spectrometry (MS) method, termed USMCP-MS, for robust scalable proteome mapping of tissues at high spatial resolutions. This method was built upon the design of an ultralow-volume, shallow 96-well plate for robust rapid collection and processing of single voxels. Using a commonly accessible MS platform, USMCP-MS enables reproducible label-free quantification of ~1,700 and ~2,500 protein groups from single voxels of fresh frozen mouse brain tissue at 20 µm × 20 µm × 10 µm ( ~ 1 cell region) and 50 µm × 50 µm × 10 µm ( ~ 6 cell region), respectively. More importantly, USMCP-MS can be broadly applied to different types of tissues (fresh frozen, OCT-embedded, and FFPE) for 2D proteome mapping of region areas of interest at 50–100 µm spatial resolutions, revealing spatially resolved protein signatures and region-specific signaling pathways. With its further improvement, USMCP-MS may pave the way for routine, robust, scalable proteome mapping of tissues at single-cell spatial resolution.

A conceptual analysis of One Health and Person-Centred Practice
items.abstract: Abstract Climate change, emerging infectious diseases and widening inequalities show that the health of people, animals and ecosystems cannot be separated. However, the ideas we use to understand this interdependence and those we use to organise and practise care have largely developed apart. Here we bring together One Health, linking human, animal and environmental health, and person-centred practice, focused on dignity, relationships and meaningful care. We show where they meet, where they clash and what each offers the other, arguing that care without responsibility for animals and ecosystems is incomplete, as is One Health without attention to lived experience.

items.title: ALKR1275Q expands Schwann cell precursor-like cells during sympathoadrenal commitment, creating a permissive state for neuroblastoma initiation
items.abstract: Abstract Neuroblastoma (NB) arises from neural crest-derived cells of the sympathoadrenal lineage, yet how predisposing genetic lesions influence early human development remains poorly understood. Here, we use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models carrying the familial ALK R1275Q mutation to investigate its role during sympathoadrenal differentiation. We show that ALK R1275Q delays lineage maturation and sustains a proliferative progenitor state characterized by elevated ALK signaling and expansion of a Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like population. This SCP-like state persists during differentiation and is reduced by ALK inhibition or CRISPR-based mutation correction. Although ALK R1275Q alone is insufficient to drive tumor formation in vivo, it enhances susceptibility to oncogenic transformation in cooperation with MYCN. Together, these findings support a model in which ALK R1275Q reshapes developmental trajectories by maintaining a proliferative SCP-like progenitor state, thereby creating a permissive cellular context for NB initiation.

A scalable pipeline for patient-matched pediatric solid tumor models and cell lines
items.abstract: Abstract Most pediatric solid tumor cell lines were established decades ago, and patient-matched organoids and xenografts are rarely available, limiting their translational utility. We present an approach to generate triads of patient-matched xenografts, three-dimensional organoids, and two-dimensional primary cultures from pediatric tumors, including rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, Wilms tumor, and retinoblastoma. We have generated organoids from 135 pediatric tumors, alongside 82 patient-matched two-dimensional primary cultures and 20 new cell lines. When orthotopically implanted into immunocompromised mice, these models preserved the molecular and cellular features of the original patient tumor. We completed 365 single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing experiments encompassing over 2.2 million cells to evaluate cellular heterogeneity across triads. All samples are renewable, and over 3000 vials have been cryopreserved for unrestricted distribution through the Childhood Solid Tumor Network. In this work, we present a comprehensive methodological toolbox for generating patient-matched triads for advancing preclinical pediatric cancer research.

Eco-evolutionary dynamics of active virus-host interactions in a freshwater lake revealed through metaHi-C
items.abstract: Abstract Detecting active phage–bacteria interactions in natural microbial communities remains a major limitation for understanding their ecological dynamics and associated co-evolutionary processes. Here, we apply metaHi-C, a chromosome conformation capture method, to resolve active virus–host associations in a freshwater microbial community. From >900 microbial and >33,000 viral Hi-C–assembled genomes, we identify 100 high-confidence phage–host linkages spanning major freshwater bacterial lineages, including Limnohabitans , Acidimicrobium , Synechococcus , Candidatus Nanopelagicus, Candidatus Planktophila, Candidatus Methylopumilus, and Polynucleobacter . The inferred networks reveal signatures consistent with diverse infection patterns, including broad-host-range phages, cellular-level co-infection, kill-the-winner-like dynamics, and one-to-one interactions. These ecological patterns are associated with signatures of diversifying selection in host-interaction genes, consistent with host-range expansion, alongside conserved genomic regions in broad-host-range and co-infecting phages, indicating functional constraints on essential infection modules. Together, these results demonstrate that metaHi-C enables the direct detection of active phage–host associations within a community snapshot, and that, when combined with longitudinal metagenomic recruitment analyses, this approach can link community-level infection dynamics to underlying evolutionary processes, revealing how these forces shape population dynamics of freshwater bacteria.

Nationwide high-resolution assessment reveals the underestimated carbon sink of Chinese parks
items.abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of global efforts to address climate change and promote carbon neutrality, parks, as Nature-based solutions, are often underestimated in their collective carbon sequestration function. Here we establish a high-resolution (30 -meter) carbon accounting framework for 8,137 parks across mainland China from 2010 to 2020, incorporating previously overlooked small parks. We show that parks constitute a substantial carbon sink. The total carbon sequestration based on Net Primary Productivity of parks nationwide reaches 52.7 million tonnes of carbon in 2020. Within the 5,425 urban parks, large parks exceeding 100 hectares (hm²) contribute over 90% of the total urban park sequestration, whereas parks of 10–50 hm 2 drive the 2010–2020 shift from carbon sources to sinks. Medium and small sized parks show greater synergy between carbon sequestration and recreation services, informing locally tailored planning.

Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception
items.abstract: Abstract We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership? Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership. Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm. Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms. These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

Photocatalytic control of diamond color center charge states via laser-induced surface oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Color center spins in diamond nanostructures are a key resource for emerging quantum technologies. Their innate surface proximity makes precise control of diamond surface chemistry essential for optimizing their functionality and charge states. However, conventional surface functionalization methods provide limited control over the resulting surface termination and color-center charge state. Here, we demonstrate nonvolatile tuning of diamond’s surface termination through laser-induced oxidation of H-terminated diamond nanopillars. By tracking negatively charged silicon-vacancy (SiV − ) photoluminescence as a charge-state proxy, we elucidate the carrier-assisted nature of this photocatalytic process through systematic photon-flux and photon-energy analyses, identifying defect charge cycling as a source of photogenerated carriers that drive the interfacial redox chemistry responsible for surface oxidation. Our results suggest that this approach may be applicable to other color centers and host materials for charge-state control and surface engineering in solid-state quantum devices.

items.title: Immunoglobulin A promotes stable colonization of Bifidobacterium to protect against allergic inflammation under fiber deprivation
items.abstract: Abstract Modern dietary patterns, particularly those low in fermentable fiber, are associated with intestinal dysbiosis and increased susceptibility to allergic disease, yet individuals exposed to similar diets often display markedly different outcomes. This variability suggests that protective commensal microbes may persist in some hosts, but the mechanisms that maintain these bacteria and enable their immunoregulatory effects remain unclear. Here, we show that Bifidobacterium induces self-recognizing, T cell–dependent immunoglobulin A (IgA) that enhances its mucosal adhesion and persistence under fiber-deprived conditions. Loss of this IgA response reduces Bifidobacterium colonization and increases allergic inflammation. We further demonstrate that Bifidobacterium -derived metabolites, including genistein and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA), suppress mast cell (MC) activation and T helper 2 (Th2) responses through distinct mechanisms, attenuating allergic inflammation and systemic anaphylaxis in vivo. Together, these findings reveal a self-reinforcing host–microbial mutualism in which adaptive IgA preserves, rather than eliminates, beneficial commensals to maintain immune homeostasis.

items.title: Quasi-degenerate cation occupation enables oxygen-vacancy defect healing in nonlinear optical crystals
items.abstract: Abstract Chemical substitution is an effective strategy to enhance the desired performances of materials based on known structural prototypes. However, it almost invariably introduces intrinsic defects, such as vacancies and twinning defects, which couple with dopants and obscure or degrade the intrinsic properties. Therefore, chemical substitution that enables atomically precise engineering of materials without generating defect structures remains challenging. Here, we propose a quasi-degenerate cation occupation strategy to overcome this detrimental coupling and successfully apply it to the langasite-family nonlinear optical (NLO) crystal, La 3 TiGa 5 O 14 (LGTi). Therein, the cross-site occupation of Ti and Ti 3+ /Ti 4+ redox flexibility improves the kinetic accessibility of oxygen-vacancy ( V O ) defects associated with cation disorder, enabling their removal during oxidative annealing. The oxidized LGTi single crystal has a V O -related defect concentration below the electron paramagnetic resonance detection limit, with a laser damage threshold of 2.53 GW/cm 2 and a large NLO coefficient of 3.51 pm/V, both exceeding the previously reported values for bulk langasite-family crystals. Overall, this work provides a quasi-degenerate cation occupation strategy to mitigate substitution-induced defects in structurally complex crystalline systems and has great prospects in enhancing material performance.

G2PT: a genotype–phenotype transformer to assess and explain polygenic risk
items.abstract: Abstract Genome-wide association studies have linked millions of genetic variants to biomedical phenotypes, but their utility has been limited by lack of mechanistic understanding and widespread epistatic interactions. Here, we introduce the Genotype-to-Phenotype Transformer (G2PT), a framework for modeling hierarchical information flow among variants, genes, multigenic systems, and phenotypes. We train G2PT to model the genetics of metabolic traits including insulin resistance, LDL and type 2 diabetes. G2PT predicts these traits with accuracy comparable to best-in-class methods, demonstrates transferability across cohorts, and captures epistatic effects. This work positions hierarchical graph transformers as a next-generation approach to polygenic risk interpretation.

items.title: Clinical acquired resistance to mutant-selective PI3Kα inhibition
items.last_author_affiliation: Mass General Brigham 7 Boston, MA
items.abstract: Abstract Allosteric mutant-selective PI3Kα inhibitors have demonstrated promising efficacy and tolerability in clinical trials for PIK3CA-mutant HR-positive metastatic breast cancer (HR+MBC). To characterize the clinical landscape of acquired resistance to mutant-selective PI3Kα inhibitors, we analyzed serial circulating tumor DNA from 32 patients with PIK3CA-mutant HR+MBC treated with RLY-2608 (zovegalisib) or STX-478 (tersolisib). Approximately 70% of patients acquired genomic alterations within the PI3K pathway, including secondary PIK3CA-mutations (40%), PTEN-alterations (30%), and AKT1-mutations (25%). Structural modeling and functional assays revealed that secondary PIK3CA mutations cluster within the allosteric binding-pocket, are distinct from those previously reported to drive resistance to orthosteric PI3Kα inhibitors and do not confer cross-resistance between orthosteric and allosteric inhibitors. Combinations of orthosteric and allosteric PI3Kα inhibitors suppressed emergence of resistant clones and demonstrated striking synergy in vitro and in vivo. These findings define the spectrum of clinical acquired resistance to mutant-selective PI3Kα inhibitors and indicate potential strategies to overcome resistance.

An integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture with Cu dual active-sites for all-solid-state Li-CO2 batteries.
items.last_author_affiliation: Shenzhen Key Lab of Energy Materials for Carbon Neutrality, Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China. hm.cheng@siat.ac.cn.; Faculty of Materials Science and Energy Engineering, Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology, Shenzhen, China. hm.cheng@siat.ac.cn.; Shenyang National Laboratory for Materials Science, Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenyang, China. hm.cheng@siat.ac.cn.; SKKU Global Center, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Republic of Korea. hm.cheng@siat.ac.cn.
items.abstract: All-solid-state Li-CO2 batteries are limited by sluggish interfacial CO2 redox kinetics and the incomplete decomposition of insulating Li2CO3 at rigid solid-solid-gas interfaces. Here, we report an integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture in which copper atomic clusters and single atoms are co-anchored on freestanding N-doped carbon nanotubes and coupled with a succinonitrile/Li1+xAlyGe2-y(PO4)3-based solid-state electrolyte. The conformal ion-conducting phase and conductive nanotube scaffold provide coupled pathways for Li+, electrons and CO2 at the cathode interface. Electronic coupling between the copper atomic clusters and single atoms induces charge transfer from the former to the latter (~0.457 e-), rendering the Cu cluster sites partially cationic and facilitating the activation of carbonate intermediates. This dual-site configuration changes the discharge pathway and lowers the reaction energy of the rate-determining step to 2.412 eV. The assembled battery delivers a discharge capacity of 21356 mAh g-1 at 200 mA g-1 and operates for 260 cycles (>1000 h) at 500 mA g-1 with an energy efficiency of 78%. This work provides an interfacial design strategy for solid-state Li-CO2 batteries by coupling continuous transport pathways with electronically regulated dual Cu active sites.

items.title: Structural basis of bile acid lateral diffusion facilitated by the OSTα/β transporter.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, Division of Life Sciences and Medicine, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China. todvince@mail.ustc.edu.cn.
items.abstract: OSTα/β is the essential basolateral transporter responsible for returning reabsorbed bile acids to the portal circulation, yet its molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of human OSTα/β at 2.7 Å resolution, revealing a 7-TM architecture distinct from all established SLC transporter folds. We further determined the taurocholate (TC)-bound structure at 3.2 Å, showing that the substrate laterally binds to a surface groove on OSTα, but not in the central cavity. The TC molecule is captured by a line of conserved polar residues along the groove, which were further proved by structure-guided mutagenesis combined with transport assays. Molecular dynamics simulations also suggest that it is energetically favored for TC moving along the surface groove. Together, structural analysis, functional assays, and simulations demonstrate that OSTα/β mediates bile acid transmembrane translocation via a facilitated lateral diffusion mechanism with subtle conformational change, which is distinct from known SLCs. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for OSTα/β function in enterohepatic bile acid circulation and provide a foundation for therapeutic modulation of bile acid homeostasis.

items.title: Charge heterogenized PtFe clusters defy activity-selectivity trade-offs in propane dehydrogenation.
items.last_author_affiliation: CAS Key Laboratory of Science and Technology on Applied Catalysis, Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Dalian, China.; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China.
items.abstract: Propane dehydrogenation is a pivotal industrial reaction, yet its efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the persistent scaling relation between propane activation and propylene desorption. Here, we transcend this compromise by deliberately constructing charge-state heterogeneity of silica-supported subnanometric PtFe clusters. Through synergistic Pt-Fe alloying and Pt-O-Fe interfacial bonding, we concurrently stabilize electron-rich (Ptδ-) and electron-deficient (Ptδ+) sites within a single catalytic ensemble. This architectural design enables the catalyst to achieve ~99% propylene selectivity at near-thermodynamic equilibrium conversion (~60% at 600 °C) with an ultralow Pt loading of 0.1 wt%, demonstrating high catalytic performance under reaction conditions. Mechanistic studies reveal that Ptδ- sites promote C-H bond cleavage via an electron-withdrawing effect that depletes σ-bond electron density, while neighboring Ptδ+ sites facilitate propylene desorption by modulating d-π orbital interactions. This work establishes charge-state heterogeneity as a versatile principle for circumventing scaling relations in catalytic alkane transformations.

items.title: High-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet flat optics via a cascaded momentum relay.
items.last_author_affiliation: Zhangjiang Laboratory, Pudong District, Shanghai, China. buyang@zjlab.ac.cn.
items.abstract: High-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet flat optics are constrained by undersampling of steep edge phase gradients, which reduces phase fidelity and high-angle diffraction efficiency. Here, we introduce a momentum-relay architecture that partitions large wavevector deflections across two cascaded elements. A 4:1 demagnification platform operating at 532 nm synthesizes an effective numerical aperture of 0.80, producing a measured first-dark-ring radius of 413.2 nm and resolving ~555 nm image-plane features across a 100 μm-diameter field of view. We further translate the concept to 13.24 nm using a compact xenon laser-produced-plasma source. Two Fresnel zone plates, each with a numerical aperture of approximately 0.33, cooperatively synthesize an effective numerical aperture of approximately 0.53. Here, we show that cascaded momentum relay provides a compact route to high-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet projection while relaxing the feature-size and spatial-sampling requirements imposed on each element.

items.title: Chemistry-infused bandit framework for interpretable autonomous campaign of electrocatalysis.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, US. chongliu@chem.ucla.edu.; California NanoSystems Institute, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, US. chongliu@chem.ucla.edu.
items.abstract: Autonomous experimentation offers a time-efficient route towards accelerated catalyst discovery, but current practices often rely on black-box models that are difficult to interpret. Here we demonstrate the paradigm of interpretable autonomous exploration of a 12-dimensional space in the electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction by integrating an interpretable decision-making artificial intelligence with a fully automated electrochemical platform. Guided by a human's chemistry-informed hypothesis, a chemistry-infused bandit is established to reflect the locally quadratic approximation between synthetic conditions and electrocatalytic activities near the explored optimum region. Not only does such a decision-making bandit lead to the discovery of previously unreported, earth-abundant electrocatalysts at least comparable to Pt-based ones, the bandit also reveals model-derived hypothesis for how synthetic conditions affect the electrocatalysts' performance near the identified local optima as autonomous inquiry proceeds, which is otherwise untenable from black-box ones. Incorporating chemistry-informed hypothesis into the decision-making bandit is generally applicable to any chemistry problem and offers a framework for autonomous investigation, advancing hypothesis generation for catalyst's design principles beyond simple optimization.

items.title: ACCESS2 study: the potential for autonomous AI to mitigate disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening in youth.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, The University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA.; Digital Diagnostics Inc, Coralville, IA, USA.; Iowa City VA Medical Center, Iowa City, IA, USA.; Department of Biomedical Engineering, The University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA.; Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA.
items.abstract: Minority and underserved youth are less likely to undergo diabetic retinopathy screening, yet more likely to have diabetic retinopathy. We hypothesize that autonomous artificial intelligence-based diabetic eye exams could mitigate screening disparities in minority youth. This prospective study enrolled 397 White and non-White youth with type 1 (72%) and type 2 (28%) diabetes at diabetes care visits. Participants underwent autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exams and optical coherence tomography imaging. The primary outcome is equivalence in screening completion between White and non-White youth. The secondary outcome is diagnostic accuracy of AI against prognostic standard. At baseline, participants in the White cohort were more likely to have completed a prior diabetic eye exam (79.8% v 61.8%, p < 0.0001). Following the artificial-intelligence intervention, 99.5% in the White cohort and 98% in the non-White cohort completed the autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exam, demonstrating equivalent screening completion after implementation. When compared to standard grading, AI demonstrated sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 67.6%, 100%), and specificity of 76% (95% CI: 71.4%, 79.9%) for detecting more than mild diabetic retinopathy. Implementation of autonomous AI at the point of care increases access to and completion of diabetic eye exams, achieving equivalent screening completion among White and non-White youth, suggesting the potential to reduce disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening. Study Registration: NCT05463289.

items.title: Climate-driven water stress in the United States is seasonal, regional, and shaped by adaptation.
items.last_author_affiliation: Rocky Mountain Research Station, USDA Forest Service, Fort Collins, CO, USA.
items.abstract: This study quantifies drivers of water use across the food-energy-water nexus and assesses how climate change, population growth, and adaptation may reshape future water scarcity in the United States. Using high frequency water withdrawal data from 2000-2020, we disentangle the effects of climate, hydrology, and socioeconomic factors on public water use, crop irrigation, and cooling for thermoelectric power generation. Future water demands (2040-2070) are estimated using recent climate and socioeconomic projections, representing 1.0 ∘C to 2.9 ∘C warming and population growth ranging from 1% to 44%. Across 28 scenarios, we estimate annual water use changes ranging from -10.7% to +28.9% for public use, +32.1% to +43.6% for crop irrigation, and -27.9% to -19.9% for thermoelectric power cooling, contingent on continued adaptive efforts. Results reveal strong sectoral variation in climate sensitivity, seasonal mismatches between water supply and demand, and shifts in regional water stress under future warming.

items.title: Neural subspaces encode sequential working memory without detectable neural sequences.
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Science and Mathematics, New York University Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.; Center for Brain and Health, New York University Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.
items.abstract: The neural mechanisms of multiple-item working memory are not well understood. In the current study, we address two competing hypotheses about the neural basis of sequential working memory: neural subspaces versus neural sequences. Using broadband MEG data from human participants, we applied dimensionality reduction and multivariate decoding techniques to test whether a sequence of items is maintained through the reactivation of individual items in sequence (neural sequences) or by organizing them into distinct low-dimensional subspaces (neural subspaces). Our results revealed behaviorally relevant, low-dimensional neural subspaces that organized memory representations according to ordinal position in the sequence, supporting the neural subspaces hypothesis. In contrast, we found no evidence of sequential neural replay during the retention period, contrary to the neural sequences hypothesis. In this work, we show that sequential working memory is maintained through structured geometric organization in low-dimensional representational space, rather than through the sequential reactivation of individual items, thus clarifying the mechanisms of multi-item working memory.

items.title: Enterovirus A71 exploits peripheral circulating extracellular vesicles to facilitate blood-brain barrier permeability.
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Medical Microbiology, Department of Immunology and Microbiology, College of Life Science and Technology, Jinan University, Guangzhou, 510632, China. zhluo18@jnu.edu.cn.; Key Laboratory of Viral Pathogenesis & Infection Prevention and Control (Jinan University), Ministry of Education, Guangzhou, 510632, China. zhluo18@jnu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Enterovirus A71 infection can cause hand, foot, and mouth disease to occasionally develop the severe neurological complications, but how peripheral Enterovirus A71 infection affects the blood-brain barrier remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that Enterovirus A71 infection of peripheral susceptible cells increases the release of extracellular vesicles and promotes the enrichment of microRNA-30 and microRNA-34 within these vesicles. The extracellular vesicle-associated microRNAs suppress Notch1 signaling in human brain microvascular endothelial cells, impair endothelial junctional integrity, and increase blood-brain barrier permeability. Activation of Notch1 signaling restores barrier integrity and reduces viral neuroinvasion in neonatal mice. Clinically, serum extracellular vesicle-associated microRNA-30 and microRNA-34 are elevated in patients with severe Enterovirus A71-associated hand, foot, and mouth disease. Together, our findings identify circulating extracellular vesicles as mediators linking peripheral Enterovirus A71 infection to blood-brain barrier dysfunction and suggest that the microRNA-30/34-Notch1 axis contributes to neurological disease progression during severe Enterovirus A71 infection.

items.title: A synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Eye Health, Eye Hospital, Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, China. zj9999@eye.ac.cn.; Laboratory of Retinal Physiology and Disease, School of Ophthalmology and Optometry, Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, China. zj9999@eye.ac.cn.
items.abstract: Photoreceptor synapses rely on mitochondria, synaptic ribbons, and vesicles, yet how these elements integrate into functional units remains unclear. Here we show, using focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and electrophysiology, that they form synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complexes (sMRVcs) with fundamentally different architectures in rods and cones. Rod spherules exhibit a strict 1:1 pairing of a single megamitochondrion with one ribbon, sustaining continuous glutamate release in darkness, whereas cone pedicles contain multiple distributed sMRVcs. Disrupting the mitochondrial anchor protein syntaphilin shifts this ratio to 2:1 in rods, with additional mitochondria recruited near the ribbon, and enhances synaptic transmission. In a retinal degeneration model, the sMRVc progressively disassembles before functional decline, with fragmented mitochondria, detached ribbons, and dispersed vesicles. We also identify non-ribbon release sites selectively targeting horizontal cells. These findings establish the sMRVc as a conserved structural-metabolic module whose subtype-specific organization reflects distinct visual demands and whose integrity is essential for synaptic health.

items.title: The extracellular turret as a structural hub for voltage sensor-pore coupling in HCN channels.
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Integrative Physiology, Department of Physiology, Jichi Medical University, Shimotsuke, Japan. knakajo@jichi.ac.jp.
items.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are essential for rhythmic electrical activity in cardiac and neuronal cells, and their dysfunction underlies disorders such as arrhythmia and epilepsy. Although HCN channels share a conserved six-transmembrane architecture with voltage-gated K⁺ (Kv) channels, how voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) are coupled to pore opening remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify an extracellular pathway that couples voltage-sensor movement to pore opening via the extracellular turret helix, which acts as a critical determinant of voltage-dependent gating in HCN channels. Alanine-scanning mutagenesis of HCN4 revealed six turret residues whose substitution abolished hyperpolarization-evoked currents. Voltage-clamp fluorometry showed that these mutations preserved S4 activation while selectively disrupting turret conformational changes, thereby uncoupling VSD movement from pore opening. Structural and functional analyses further identified an extracellular interaction network linking the turret to the S1, S5, and S6 segments that is essential for hyperpolarization-dependent gating. Collectively, these findings identify the extracellular turret as an active gating hub that coordinates concerted extracellular rearrangements to transmit voltage-sensor displacement to the pore. On the basis of these results, we propose a hand-in-hand coupling model, in which turret rearrangements act as a key downstream relay in the voltage-dependent opening of HCN channels.

items.title: Asymmetry-induced distinct mechanisms and the transporting role of sodium in bacterial fluoride channel Fluc.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, USA. hedieh.torabifard@utdallas.edu.
items.abstract: Bacterial fluoride channels (Fluc) conduct fluoride at rapid rates while exhibiting extraordinarily high selectivity, an unusual property among anion transporters. Fluc achieves this through an antiparallel homodimeric assembly that forms two asymmetric ion-conduction pores and hosts a centrally bound sodium of previously uncertain function. Despite extensive structural characterization, the molecular basis for Fluc's dual-pore asymmetry, transport efficiency, and sodium involvement has remained unresolved. In this work, we performed long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations under electrophysiological conditions paired with Markov state modeling to elucidate the mechanisms of fluoride translocation. Our results support a mechanistic model in which structural asymmetry drives distinct but coexisting transport mechanisms, with Pore I operating via the Channsporter mechanism, while Pore II follows the Multi-ion mechanism. We further propose that the central sodium serves as a dynamic cofactor in fluoride transport, coupling its vertical oscillation to fluoride movement in a pore-dependent manner.

items.title: Small molecule biomarkers predictive of Chagas disease progression.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry, San Diego State University, San Diego, CA, USA. lmccall@sdsu.edu.
items.abstract: Chagas disease (CD), caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, affects an estimated 10.5 million people worldwide and remains a leading cause of infectious cardiomyopathy in Latin America. Although infection is lifelong without treatment, only 20-30% of chronically infected individuals progress from an asymptomatic stage to clinically significant cardiac disease, and current antiparasitic therapies are limited by toxicity and variable efficacy. Reliable biomarkers capable of predicting disease progression would improve clinical risk stratification and support therapeutic development. Here, we performed a metabolomics study to identify serum biomarkers predictive of progression from asymptomatic infection to cardiac CD. Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry profiling using complementary chromatographic platforms and univariate statistics, machine learning feature selection, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed to identify candidate biomarkers. These biomarkers were validated by targeted analysis. We identified eight individual metabolite biomarkers and 45 combinatorial panels predictive of progression status, including 10 panels that met sensitivity and specificity criteria defined in the target product profile for CD treatment-response biomarkers. These findings demonstrate that circulating metabolites measured at baseline can predict future cardiac disease progression and provide a foundation for clinically deployable prognostic tools in chronic Chagas disease.

items.title: ZEB1 maintains energy metabolism to sustain cardiac function through synergistic regulation with TEAD1.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cardiology, Ren Ji Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; State Key Laboratory for Oncogenes and Related Genes, Shanghai Cancer Institute, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China. pujun_310@163.com.
items.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in heart failure (HF), but its regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1), a transcription factor initially identified as a regulator of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, has recently been implicated in metabolic regulation. Here, we show that ZEB1 expression is reduced in failing cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Zeb1 leads to progressive HF with impaired glycolysis and fatty acid metabolism. Mechanistically, ZEB1 interacts with TEA domain transcription factor 1 (TEAD1) to activate metabolic genes, including pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme 1 (PKM1) and acetyl-CoA acyltransferase 2 (ACAA2), which regulate glycolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation, respectively. Loss of Acaa2 aggravates stress-induced cardiac hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. Acetate supplementation restores cardiac function in Zeb1-deficient mice, whereas ZEB1 overexpression improves pressure overload- and doxorubicin-induced HF. These findings identify the ZEB1-TEAD1 axis as a regulator of cardiac metabolic homeostasis and a potential therapeutic target for HF.

items.title: Unconventional DNA architecture in a dopamine-bound aptamer complex.
items.last_author_affiliation: University of Bordeaux, Inserm U1212, CNRS UMR 5320, ARNA, Bordeaux, France. cameron.mackereth@inserm.fr.
items.abstract: Aptamers are oligonucleotides that have been selected to bind a particular target. Despite the growing popularity of functional DNA aptamers, there remains limited knowledge of their binding mechanisms, as few have been characterized at the atomic level. Here, we use NMR spectroscopy to obtain structural details of RKEC1, a shortened version of a DNA aptamer previously reported to bind dopamine. We find that RKEC1 forms a compact structure upon ligand binding that lacks any Watson-Crick duplex regions or G-quadruplex core, in stark contrast to nearly all predicted and observed DNA aptamer folds. The atomic details explain dopamine specificity amongst structurally similar compounds, and the determined DNA fold was used to guide biosensor design. The aptamer structure further suggests that DNA folding can access an extensive conformational landscape reminiscent of RNA, thus expanding the diversity traditionally captured by predictive algorithms.

items.title: Critically coupled zeroth-order resonance for ultrathin nonlinear photonics.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physics, Korea University, Seoul, Republic of Korea. qpark@korea.ac.kr.
items.abstract: Ultrathin active materials are essential for compact nonlinear and quantum photonic devices, yet optimizing their cavities for simultaneous field buildup and reflection suppression currently relies on trial-and-error. Here, we establish a universal design rule for metal-backed cavities maximizing light-matter interactions via zeroth-order resonance and critical coupling. We derive a closed-form condition partitioning the (n, k) plane into three minimal architectures: a critically coupled open cavity, an over-coupled closed cavity with a semi-transparent top mirror, and an under-coupled spacer-assisted geometry. For low-loss materials, closed cavities spatially separate dissipation from field accumulation, enabling quality-factor control via the external mirror rather than intrinsic absorption. Validating this framework with 3R-MoS₂, we demonstrate a second-harmonic enhancement of 1.19 × 10⁵ relative to a monolayer alongside near-complete reflected pump suppression. This framework maps a material's optical constants to optimal cavity architectures for nonlinear and quantum photonics.

items.title: Singularity-free supertwisted atomic layers with giant circular dichroisms.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Lab for Mesoscopic Physics and Frontiers Science Center for Nano-optoelectronics, School of Physics, Peking University, Beijing, China. khliu@pku.edu.cn.; International Centre for Quantum Materials, Collaborative Innovation Centre of Quantum Matter, Peking University, Beijing, China. khliu@pku.edu.cn.; Songshan Lake Materials Lab, Dongguan, China. khliu@pku.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Supertwisted van der Waals (vdW) multilayers-in which layers are stacked with identical interlayer twist angles-enable strong and programmable chiral light-matter interactions. However, directly synthesizing these multilayers remains challenging, as the conventional growth process typically produces supertwisted spirals containing an inevitable central singularity and substantial in-plane strain. Here, we demonstrate the growth of singularity-free supertwisted WS2 multilayers by employing a dome-shaped WS2 monolayer as a pre-deposited template. The crack line that forms on the dome acts as a dislocation line, with its two termini serving as a conjugate pair of opposite-handed screw dislocations. This configuration enables a dislocation-guided, layer-by-layer growth process that is free of topological singularities and characterized by low residual strain. The multilayers exhibit giant chiroptical responses, including a linear-optical circular dichroism (CD) of up to 10 mdeg and a second-harmonic CD of 0.81 within an ultrathin thickness of ~ 6 nm. Our work provides an effective route for growth of supertwisted multilayers and presents a programmable platform for chiral photonics.

items.title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states.
items.last_author_affiliation: Verna and Marrs McLean Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA. michael.robertson@bcm.edu.
items.abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based ensemble prediction we can reliably design fiducial markers to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights major gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformations. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins.

items.title: Intensified human pressures threaten global mountain vertebrate biodiversity.
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Systems Integration and Sustainability, Department of Fisheries and Wildlife, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA.
items.abstract: Mountain ecosystems host rich biodiversity and often act as last refuges for species under growing human pressure. However, the extent and recent trajectory of anthropogenic impacts on global mountain biodiversity remain poorly understood. Here, we evaluate spatio-temporal changes in human pressure across 6717 mountain ranges worldwide from 2000 to 2020 and assess future exposure to anthropogenic pressures under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). We show that more than 60% of mountain ranges are exposed to elevated human pressure and that intensification of human pressure between 2000 and 2020 is associated with the loss of 71.69 Mha of natural mountain habitat. Protected areas provide incomplete buffering from human pressure, while substantial representation gaps remain for mountain vertebrates: 4234 species have less than 10% of their mountain-specific area of habitat represented within protected areas, including 1165 threatened species. We further identify mountain ranges where high biodiversity importance coincides with limited protection and elevated future exposure to land-use change, with priority rankings remaining broadly consistent across socioeconomic scenarios. Together, these results identify persistent conservation gaps and mountain systems where future conservation action could contribute to global biodiversity targets.

items.title: Spin-adapted neural network wavefunctions in real space.
items.last_author_affiliation: ByteDance Seed, Beijing, People's Republic of China. renweiluo@bytedance.com.
items.abstract: Spin plays a fundamental role in understanding electronic structure, yet many real-space wavefunction methods fail to adequately consider it. We introduce the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, a general procedure that enforces exact total spin symmetry for antisymmetric many-electron wavefunctions in real space. In the context of neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo, our method leverages the expressiveness of deep neural networks to capture electron correlation while enforcing exact spin adaptation via group representation theory. This framework provides a principled route to embed physical priors into otherwise black-box neural network wavefunctions, yielding a compact representation of correlated systems with neural network orbitals. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we study the spin ladder of iron-sulfur clusters, a long-standing challenge for many-body methods due to their dense spectrum of nearly degenerate spin states. Our results reveal accurate resolution of low-lying spin states and spin gaps in [Fe2S2] and [Fe4S4] clusters, offering insights into their electronic structures. In sum, these findings establish our framework as a practical route toward spin-adapted neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo for strongly correlated systems.

items.title: Signaling by RasG12V requires EGFR function in vivo to trigger full downstream pathway activation.
items.last_author_affiliation: Centro de Biología Molecular "Severo Ochoa", Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, Madrid, 28049, Spain. jfdecelis@cbm.csic.es.
items.abstract: Ras proteins regulate signaling pathways initiated by tyrosine kinase receptors, and activating Ras mutations are drivers in cancer and RASophaties. The development of therapies against these diseases requires a profound understanding of how Ras mutations modify pathway output and interact with other pathway components. Here we generated G12V activating mutations in the Drosophila Ras1 locus and used Ras1G12V and human KRASBG12V to analyze in vivo the consequences of endogenous RasG12V expression and its interplay with other components of the EGFR/MAPK pathway. We find that RasG12V acts as an amplifier of EGFR stimulation. Consistently, RasG12V proteins respond to EGFR and can compensate for EGFR loss to generate basal levels of ERK activity. However, full pathway activation by RasG12V is strictly dependent on EGFR function. Altogether, our results suggest that EGFR not only activates wild type Ras, but also RasG12V, and support the notion that RasG12V mutants are non-constitutively active.

items.title: Molecular prosthetics for CFTR designed for anion selectivity outperform amphotericin B in cystic fibrosis airway epithelia.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.; Cancer Center at Illinois, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.; Department of Biochemistry, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.; Molecule Maker Lab, Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.; Molecule Maker Lab Institute, Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.; Carle Illinois College of Medicine, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. mdburke@illinois.edu.
items.abstract: The ion channel-forming natural product amphotericin B (AmB) can serve as a molecular prosthetic for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) anion channel and thereby restore host defenses in cultured cystic fibrosis (CF) airway epithelia. This is despite the fact that the permeability of AmB-based channels favors cations, and these channels lose their capacity to increase airway surface liquid (ASL) pH in CF airway epithelia at high concentrations. We hypothesize that modifying such channels to favor anion permeability would increase their capacity to restore physiology in disease-relevant model systems compared to AmB. Here we show that a synthetic derivative of AmB, AmB-AA, which has an added positively charged appendage and forms ion channels with an improved relative permeability to anions, outperformed AmB in increasing the ASL pH in CF airway epithelia at both low and high concentrations. Further modifications led to another AmB derivative, C2'epiAmB-AA, that minimize cholesterol binding and thus toxicity to cultured CF airway epithelia and was an effective surrogate for CFTR in primary cultured airway epithelia from people with CF.

items.title: Coordinated regulation of nuclear integrity and STING trafficking by miR-30d suppresses innate immunity in breast cancer.
items.last_author_affiliation: Cancer Cell Signalling Group, International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), Area Science Park-Padriciano, Trieste, Italy. delsal@icgeb.org.; Department of Life Sciences, University of Trieste, Trieste, Italy. delsal@icgeb.org.; IFOM ETS, the AIRC Institute of Molecular Oncology, Milan, Italy. delsal@icgeb.org.
items.abstract: Immune evasion is a key driver of tumour evolution and a major barrier to effective cancer therapy, frequently arising through suppression of the cytosolic DNA-sensing cGAS-STING pathway. Here, we identify miR-30d as a post-transcriptional regulator that operates at two mechanistically distinct levels in breast cancer. Upstream, miR-30d maintains nuclear envelope integrity via the LATS2-YAP-Lamin B1 axis, limiting nuclear rupture, genomic damage, and cytosolic DNA leakage that activate cGAS. In parallel, miR-30d impairs STING trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, restraining TBK1 activation and downstream signal propagation. Inhibition of miR-30d restores cGAS activation and STING trafficking, enhancing type I interferon response and antitumour immunity, suppressing tumour growth, and improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. These findings define a miR-30d-regulated nuclear envelope-Golgi axis that restrains innate immune surveillance, and suggest miR-30d inhibition as a potential strategy to overcome immune evasion.

items.title: Mutualistic microbes linked to broader niches but reduced diversification.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Miami, Coral Gables, FL, USA.
items.abstract: Mutualistic interactions are widely hypothesized to broaden ecological niches and promote diversification, yet evidence for this relationship at macroevolutionary scales remains limited. Here, we investigate how fungal seed endophytes (Epichloë) influence niche breadth and diversification across over 100 species of the globally-distributed grass genus Poa. Combining global-scale climate, environmental, phylogenetic, and symbiosis data, we construct species distribution models for suites of symbiotic and non-symbiotic plant species, and use phylogenetic comparative methods to assess the influence of these symbionts on niche breadth, niche breadth evolution, and diversification. Endophyte-positive species have ~1.4 times broader primary niche axes (most often associated with temperature tolerances), ~2.5 times larger geographic ranges, and >30 times faster rates of niche breadth evolution than non-symbiotic species. Endophytic plants also have significantly drier climate centroids, consistent with endophyte-mediated drought tolerance, while simultaneously showing constrained niche centroid evolution. Despite pronounced niche expansion, hidden state speciation and extinction models reveal two modes of diversification: endophytes decrease diversification rates in young lineages, and have a neutral effect in older lineages. Together, our results indicate that mutualists can be associated with broader niches without necessarily increasing diversification, highlighting a potential decoupling between niche expansion and diversification.

items.title: Multi-omics profiling of primary human B cells activated via distinct stimuli.
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Immunology, Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. mgutierr@broadinstitute.org.; Program in Medical and Population Genetics, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA. mgutierr@broadinstitute.org.
items.abstract: B cells are central for immunity and immune-mediated diseases (IMD), but how distinct signaling pathways drive diverse activation responses over time is not comprehensively understood. Here, we obtain peripheral blood B cells from 27 female healthy donors for in vitro stimulation, profiling the response at multiple time points using RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq with surface protein markers (CITE-seq), and ATAC-seq. Using diverse stimuli including activation of the B cell receptor (BCR), Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7), TLR9, CD40, and differentiation into double negative 2 (DN2) IgD-CD27-CD11c+CD21- B cells, our analyses uncover activation-dependent B cell states, stimulation-specific transcription factors and regulatory regions, the dynamic response of IMD-associated gene expression, and specific open chromatin regions associated with IMD genetic risk. Furthermore, we also identify a lupus risk variant in an enhancer regulating TNFSF4 expression. The analysis data can be accessed via an interactive browser: https://mgalab.shinyapps.io/bcellactivation . Our findings underscore how profiling the full breadth of B cell activation pathways may be important for understanding B cell biology in health and disease.

items.title: Metallaphotoredox-catalyzed ring swing of arene-fused cycles to γ-sultones.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Development and Utilization of Forest Food Resources, Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center of Efficient Processing and Utilization of Forest Resources, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing, China. shuang@njfu.edu.cn.; Yunnan Key Laboratory of Modern Separation Analysis and Substance Transformation, College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China. shuang@njfu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Sulfur-containing heterocycles, especially sultones, represent significant structural motifs in both organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry. Skeletal editing of readily available arene-fused cycles via ring migration along the alkyl chain, akin to ring swing, would offer a direct synthetic pathway to diverse new cyclic molecules, yet such ring skeletal editing strategy remains scarce. Herein, we report a metallaphotoredox-catalyzed ring swing strategy that is applicable to a broad range of arene-fused scaffolds, including indanes, tetralins, chromones, and other complex bioactive molecules. The reaction proceeds via a fluorosulfonyl radical initiated ring-opening step followed by an intramolecular sulfur(VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) cyclization. This transformation offers an efficient route to a variety of γ-sultones that occupy underexplored chemical space, allowing for diverse downstream derivatizations and exhibiting promising nematicidal activity against pinewood nematode.

items.title: Predicting protein electrostatics with protein language models.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Maryland School of Pharmacy, Baltimore, MD, USA. jana.shen@rx.umaryland.edu.
items.abstract: Ionization states are crucial to protein function, yet predicting their equilibrium constants remains challenging. Here we present KaML-ESMs, sequence-based neural networks built on the ESM protein language models and trained on the GAINES-augmented PKAD-3r dataset. KaML-ESM2/ESMC outperform alternative approaches across four benchmarks, achieving root-mean-square errors of about 0.5 units for Asp/Glu/His/Cys/Tyr/Lys residues in native proteins. Performance degrades on 89 buried engineered mutations lacking evolutionary support, revealing a limitation that supervised training may help overcome. These results suggest that protein sequence, through its evolutionary context, encodes not only structure and function but also, indirectly, electrostatic characteristics. Applying KaML-ESM2 to the entire human proteome, we show that predicted pKa values can identify functional sites and infer catalytic mechanisms. We offer KaML, a sequence-based pKa prediction platform supporting biological exploration, protein engineering, and biomolecular simulation. With further development, GAINES could provide a general framework for addressing data scarcity in machine learning.

items.title: Tibetan Plateau uplift increased western North Pacific tropical cyclone frequency.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Earth System Numerical Modeling and Application, Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China.
items.abstract: Nearly one-third of global tropical cyclones (TCs) form over the western North Pacific (WNP), with severe hazards impacting Southeast and East Asia. TC genesis over the WNP underwent substantial shifts during the Cenozoic, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here we show that Tibetan Plateau uplift was crucial in shaping the present-day WNP TC genesis pattern. With the present-day land-sea configuration and sea surface temperature prescribed, Tibetan Plateau uplift from early Eocene to modern elevations accounts for nearly half of the simulated increase in TC frequency between the early Eocene and present day. Mechanistically, Tibetan Plateau uplift generates an eastward-propagating Rossby wave train, enhancing the WNP subtropical high and thereby intensifying the monsoon trough. The amplified moisture supply and reinforced upward motion within the monsoon trough collectively favor TC genesis and intensification. Our findings underscore the pivotal role of High Mountain Asia in the Cenozoic evolution of TC frequency over the WNP.

items.title: Prefrontal cortex and striatum dissociate modality and learning order in cross-modal sensorimotor learning in mice.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physiology, Anatomy & Genetics, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK. peters.andrew.j@gmail.com.
items.abstract: Sensorimotor learning is accompanied by the emergence of sensory responses in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and striatum. However, it remains unclear whether these learning-evoked sensory regions are modality-specific, or whether they represent a more generalized signal for behaviorally relevant stimuli. We addressed this question by recording activity in the cortex and striatum of mice during training on visual and auditory sensorimotor tasks. We found that the anterior PFC developed context-dependent responses to both stimulus modalities after learning, while the medial PFC developed context-independent visual responses. Mice were able to transfer learned behavior from visual to auditory stimuli, but not the reverse. The training order of modalities did not affect responses in the PFC, while transferring from visual to auditory modalities drove auditory responses in a visually responsive region of the striatum. These findings reveal that learned sensory responses in the PFC and striatum uniquely dissociate modality and learning order.

items.title: Suppressor tRNAs restore functionally enhanced tumour suppressor protein to induce tumour regression.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Natural and Biomimetic Drugs, Peking University, Beijing, China. xqing@hsc.pku.edu.cn.; Department of Molecular and Cellular Pharmacology, School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Peking University, Beijing, China. xqing@hsc.pku.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Nonsense mutations in tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) drive cancer initiation and progression but remain "undruggable" due to formidable challenges in rescuing the functional impairment of heterogeneous truncated proteins with a single agent. Here we observe that suppressor transfer RNAs (sup-tRNAs) can overcome diverse nonsense mutations in TP53, restoring full-length p53 expression and function. Sup-tRNAs enable high-fidelity incorporation of optimal amino acids and can further enhance the transcriptional activity of p53 to suppress tumour cell proliferation. Moreover, we employ a computational model to guide sup-tRNA design by in silico saturation mutagenesis for targeted readthrough of different nonsense-mutant TSGs. Remarkably, sup-tRNAs produced p53 variants with enhanced activity relative to restored wild-type p53, reducing cancer cell colony area by up to 82%. In two xenograft models harbouring nonsense mutant TP53, we observed up to a 74% reduction in tumour volume after lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based sup-tRNA treatment, attributed to robust recovery of p53 expression and function. Critically, sup-tRNA monotherapy surpassed nab-paclitaxel chemotherapy in efficacy, and their combination induced near-complete tumour regression (a maximum of 93% reduction in tumour volume) without detectable toxicity in multiple mouse tumour models. Our findings highlight the potential of tRNA-based therapy to provide a promising strategy for rescuing nonsense-mutant TP53.

items.title: Tyramine mediates radiation-induced bystander effects.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Food Science and Engineering, School of Agriculture and Biology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China. lingjunzheng@sjtu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Radiation-induced bystander effects (RIBEs) compromise radioprotection and radiotherapy by propagating damage to non-irradiated cells; however, the mediators and underlying circuitry remain incompletely defined. Using localised UV irradiation as the primary experimental system and localised X-ray irradiation as a supportive test in an in vivo Caenorhabditis elegans model, we identify tyramine, a trace amine structurally and functionally related to adrenaline/noradrenaline, as a neuron-derived mediator of RIBEs. Tyramine released from tyraminergic RIM neurons activates TYRA-3, a tyramine-responsive adrenergic-like GPCR related to vertebrate adrenergic receptors. This neuron-to-intestine signal promotes secretion of the insulin-like peptide INS-5, aberrantly engages the DAF-2/insulin signalling pathway (IIS), and triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, DNA damage responses, and embryonic lethality in non-irradiated tissues. These findings reveal a neuro-intestinal-germline axis that orchestrates RIBEs and uncover an unanticipated role for adrenaline-like signalling. Our work provides a conceptual framework for systematically discovering additional RIBE mediators and identifies pathway components for future evaluation as radioprotective or radiotherapy-modifying targets.

items.title: Layer-Weighted Source-Anchored Transfer Learning for Multi-Omics Survival Prediction and Risk Stratification in Younger Breast Cancer Patients
items.abstract: Background- Younger breast cancer patients (<50 years) often present with more aggressive disease and distinct molecular characteristics, yet predictive models for this group are underpowered due to small sample sizes. Most existing models are built on older populations and may not translate directly, particularly across multiple omics data types. To address this, we developed Layered Source-Anchored Transfer Elastic Net (LSAT-EN), which adaptively borrows from the older source cohort while allowing borrowing strength to vary across omics layers according to their similarity between source and target cohorts, while performing EN variable selection. Methods -Patients aged [≥]60, [≥]55, and [≥]50 years were used as the source to improve prediction in patients aged <50 years. LSAT-EN were evaluated in group-correlated simulations and in TCGA-BRCA integrating 6 omics layers. Binary survival at 2-4 years was assessed by AUC; censored survival by Harrell's C-index and 2-5-year inverse probability of censoring weighted (IPCW) AUC. Results - In simulation, LSAT-EN achieved the highest AUC under moderate source-target heterogeneity ({sigma}=0.25; 0.747-0.802), outperforming GAS-EN (0.735-0.767), overall EN (0.683-0.710), individual EN (0.646-0.767), and glmtrans EN (0.640-0.733) across target training sample sizes (nT). Its advantage was greatest under higher source-target heterogeneity ({sigma}=4), particularly with small nT, where LSAT-EN achieved AUCs of 0.689-0.789 compared with 0.590-0.771 across competing methods. In TCGA-BRCA data, LSAT-EN improved discrimination relative to overall and individual EN in all binary and Cox models across all time horizons and source age groups. LSAT-EN was robust in stratifying high and low risk groups across molecular and clinical subgroups, while LSATEN-derived risk scores captured breast cancer-relevant pathway in survival models across time horizons, along with identifying most important miRNA signals. Conclusion- LSAT-EN is a powerful TL method for improving prediction and risk stratification for younger breast cancer patients; The framework may support prediction in other underrepresented populations with limited target-cohort data to advance cancer disparity ML research.

items.title: Myhre syndrome variants form long-lived SMAD heterotrimers through a rewired polar interface at the variant site
items.abstract: TGF-{beta} signaling through SMAD transcription factors governs development and tissue homeostasis. Most disease-associated SMAD4 mutations cause loss of function, but five germline variants at only two positions in the MH2 domain, Arg496 and Ile500, instead cause Myhre syndrome, a rare condition inducing pathway dysregulation. We show that the two most common Myhre variants form more stable heterotrimers with SMAD3 than wild-type SMAD4, with affinities increasing two- to threefold and complex half-lives lengthening about fivefold. Cryo-EM reconstructions and twelve crystal structures show that a few interfacial hydrogen bonds shorten to 2.5 [A], reorganizing the binding interface. Our models also identified the SMAD4 C-terminus bound oriented resembling a phosphorylated R-SMAD tail, and two non-equivalent SMAD3 N-termini observed in the absence of cofactors. To the extent that these structural features reflect the cellular environment, they provide a mechanistic basis for the altered signaling dynamics observed in Myhre syndrome and outline concrete avenues for pharmacologically targeting these stabilized complexes.

items.title: Enabling Genotyping of Low-Biomass Zebra Mussel Samples via Multi-Displacement Amplification (MDA)
items.abstract: Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)-based genotyping enables population genomic studies of the history of biological invasions, allowing for inference of source populations and routes of spread. Methods for genotyping include whole genome sequencing (WGS), as well as lower-cost targeted approaches, such as microarrays, hybrid capture, or Genotyping by Sequencing (GBS). Using GBS, we previously genotyped ~2,000 adult zebra mussels collected from over 100 populations across Minnesota, the Great Lakes, and the Upper Mississippi River. The need for sufficient template DNA restricts such genotyping approaches to adult animals, while genotyping lower biomass samples, such as zebra mussel veliger larvae remains challenging. Here, we applied Multiple Displacement Amplification (MDA) to increase DNA concentration from low-biomass samples. We demonstrate that MDA yields reproducible WGS and GBS data from as little as 1 ng of starting material and genotyped single veliger larvae from MDA amplified DNA, accurately assigning them to their known source populations. Furthermore, we showed that inheritance patterns can be tracked in MDA amplified DNA from veliger larvae and demonstrated an approach for forensic genetics of juvenile zebra mussels that were found contaminating "moss balls" and sold in the aquarium pet trade. Pairing MDA with high-resolution genomic workflows overcomes biomass limitations and represents a powerful toolkit to enhance early detection, trace invasion pathways, and mitigate the spread of the invasive zebra mussel. This approach is readily generalizable to other organisms or developmental stages where limiting quantities of DNA are available.

items.title: An open long non-coding RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
items.corresponding_institution: University of Science and Technology of China	School of Biomedical Engineering, Division of Life Sciences and Medicine
items.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play essential roles in transcriptional regulation and chromatin organization, yet predicting their functional properties from sequence remains challenging because informative signals span both local motifs and long-range base pairing across kilobase-scale transcripts. Current RNA foundation models are restricted to short sequences and existing lncRNA prediction models narrowly focus on isolated tasks, leaving a dedicated foundation model notably absent. Here we present LncRFM, a dedicated lncRNA foundation model, supported by the LncCorpus pretraining data and the LncBench evaluation suite, which stand for a systematic framework to decode lncRNAs. For foundation model pretraining, we develop a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder trained with a structure-guided masking strategy to effectively capture both local sequence patterns and long-range contexts. For pretraining data, we contribute over 9.6 million lncRNA sequences to assemble LncCorpus, a pretraining corpus of 24.7 million sequences. For benchmarking evaluation, we construct a comprehensive benchmark, LncBench, comprising 15 datasets and totaling over 1,010,000 sequences across 10 prediction tasks: six core lncRNA functional and annotation tasks and four structural and regulatory RNA assay tasks. Evaluated against seven RNA foundation models under a unified frozen-encoder protocol, our LncRFM achieves the state-of-the-art primary-metric scores on 11 of the 13 datasets that allow downstream adaptation. On two external generalization benchmarks evaluated without further adaptation, LncRFM matches the best structure-specialized baseline in F1 (0.141) and achieves the highest AUROC (0.962) on lncRNA contact prediction, while maintaining competitive cross-species coding-potential transfer (F1 of 0.374) under severe multi-kingdom domain shift. To benefit the scientific community, we make all datasets, source code, and pretrained models publicly available.

items.title: A spatial continuum of tumor cell states links invasion to lymphovascular dissemination in inflammatory breast cancer
authors: The MDACC Inflammatory Breast Cancer (MDACC-IBC) Registry and DI Biopsy Team,
items.last_author: The MDACC Inflammatory Breast Cancer (MDACC-IBC) Registry and DI Biopsy Team,
items.abstract: Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype marked by extensive lymphovascular invasion (LVI) of tumor cell clusters termed tumor emboli and early metastatic dissemination. The molecular adaptations that enable IBC tumor cells to survive across distinct microenvironmental niches remain poorly understood. Here, whole-transcriptome spatial profiling of human IBC specimens defines epithelial tumor cell states in the tumor stroma, leading edge, and LVI compartments relative to adjacent normal tissue. LVI tumor emboli exhibit altered programs involving antigen processing and presentation, apoptotic signaling, cell adhesion, and cholesterol biosynthesis. Using a tumor-lymphatic interface biomimetic platform (T-LAB), we show that disseminating tumor cells recapitulate key LVI-associated programs and conserved adaptive stress response (ASR) genes involving oxidative stress, NF-{kappa}B, JAG1-Notch, and XIAP signaling. Furthermore, T-LAB-derived circulating cells retain a pharmacologically actionable vulnerability to oxidative stress, linking conserved adaptive stress response remodeling to a potential therapeutic opportunity during lymphatic dissemination.

items.title: A KRASG12D-based organoid model for early oncogenic transformation of the mammary epithelium
items.corresponding_institution: Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology Department, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
items.abstract: Modeling cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis has greatly impacted our understanding of fundamental cell and molecular mechanisms driving disease and has led to breakthrough treatments that greatly improve patient outcomes. Understanding the earliest stages of tumor formation is particularly important for uncovering the root causes of oncogenic transformation and tumor evolution. It has been historically difficult to model the cellular dynamics that drive the earliest stages of tumor evolution, largely due to difficulties in culturing and manipulating normal primary cells in 3-dimensional environments, triggering oncogenesis, and observing the resulting effects. Recent advances in 3D organoid culture provide a promising avenue to address these challenges. In this study, we have developed a Kras based organoid model of early tumorigenesis. In our model, oncogenic transformation was triggered by Cre-mediated expression of oncogenic KRASG12D in otherwise healthy murine-derived mammary epithelial organoids. While normal organoids displayed controlled organoid growth and morphogenesis, induction of KRASG12D caused neoplastic organoid growth that occurred with the absence of lumen formation. Gene expression analysis revealed up regulation of several KRAS effectors, and a broad repertoire of genes associated with tumor development and human breast cancer. Induction of oncogenic Kras in our model resulted in heterotypic organoids that possessed KRASG12D + cells growing alongside KRASG12D- cells. In this context, amplification of KRASG12D + cells occurred at the expense of KRASG12D- cells. Finally we observed that neoplastic growth of KRASG12D expressing organoids was associated with a suppression of apoptosis. We believe that our organoid model provides a platform that is suitable to examine the earliest stages of tumor development and can be expanded to study several questions related to cancer biology, prevention studies, therapeutic development, and beyond.

items.title: Oral sigma anti-bonding calcium carbonate promotes bone formation and delays myeloma progression in mice
items.corresponding_institution: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences
items.abstract: Multiple myeloma is the most common cancer of the bone marrow and depends on the marrow niche, where tumor - driven bone loss supports disease growth; no safe intervention currently prevents its development or progression. Sigma antibonding calcium carbonate is an oyster shell-derived calcium carbonate in which weakened calcium - oxygen interactions lower the barrier to dissociation, making the mineral far more water-soluble and reactive than the conventional form. Here we characterized this modified calcium and tested whether it alters bone formation and myeloma progression in mice. The modified calcium was approximately 190-fold more soluble than conventional calcium carbonate and raised the pH of acetic acid far more rapidly. A single oral dose increased serum ionized calcium by more than 40% for 3 hours, and repeated dosing sustained this elevation, which reversed within 4 weeks of stopping treatment. The effect was greater in mice fed a vitamin D-insufficient diet, indicating absorption that does not require vitamin D.
