Ablation experiments showed that removing individual components reduced discrimination, and a separate evaluation on 54 variants supported the contribution of fine-tuning. In a cross-domain assessment, fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data increased discrimination from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants without architectural modification. We assessed in-sample calibration, and held-out validation remains necessary. These results support further evaluation of paired-sequence generative modeling and Bayesian inference for mechanistic interpretation of splicing variants across disease contexts.

items.title: Kynurenine-AHR signaling sustains a targetable FATP2 dependency in advanced systemic mastocytosis
items.corresponding_institution: Centre de Recherches en Cancérologie de Toulouse (CRCT), Inserm U1037, CNRS U5071, Université de Toulouse, Toulouse, France.
items.abstract: Avapritinib and midostaurin have transformed the treatment of advanced systemic mastocytosis (AdvSM), yet residual neoplastic mast cells persist despite sustained KIT inhibition, through mechanisms that remain poorly understood. In a prospective cohort of patients with indolent or advanced SM, plasma metabolomic profiling identified L-kynurenine (L-kyn) as a marker of advanced disease. Transcriptomics analysis of purified bone marrow mast cells, together with single-cell RNA sequencing, further revealed coordinated activation of a tryptophan-kynurenine-aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) pathway in the neoplastic marrow compartment. In KIT D816V mast cells, L-kyn activated AHR signaling, promoted a metabolic shift toward oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation, enhanced AHR-dependent fatty acid uptake, and induced expression of FATP2 (SLC27A2), the most upregulated lipid transporter in AdvSM mast cells. L-kyn also increased plasma membrane-associated cholesterol, partly independently of AHR, whereas AHR knockdown reduced GM1-positive lipid raft abundance. Disruption of membrane sphingolipids and cholesterol impaired KIT and STAT5 phosphorylation, supporting a role for lipid raft integrity in sustaining oncogenic signaling. Neither avapritinib nor midostaurin impaired L-kyn uptake, indicating that this metabolic input persists despite KIT inhibition. Pharmacologic FATP2 inhibition with lipofermata reduced mast cell viability and disease burden in a KIT D816V xenograft model. Pharmacologic or genetic FATP2 blockade synergized with avapritinib and midostaurin in mast cell lines and primary AdvSM cells ex vivo, with limited effects on normal CD34+ progenitors., These findings identify FATP2 as a therapeutically actionable metabolic dependency in AdvSM and provide a rationale for combining FATP2 inhibition with KIT-targeted therapy.

items.title: Conditioned expectations drive false odor detection
items.abstract: Research in auditory and visual fields has shown that false percepts can emerge when perceptual priors outweigh incoming sensory information. However, the role of similar top-down mechanisms in generating false percepts in the olfactory domain is less understood. To address this, we implemented a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm in which we first individually determined the odor detection thresholds of Butanol (n = 55) using an adaptive algorithm. Participants then completed an odor detection task where on each trial one of two distinct visual cues was paired with either a supra-threshold, threshold, or sub-threshold concentration of Butanol, or no odor. In the first three trial blocks, one visual stimulus (strong cue) was paired more frequently with supra-threshold concentrations, and the other visual stimulus (weak cue) was paired more frequently with sub-threshold concentrations. In the last three blocks both cues were paired most frequently with the no odor condition. We observed significantly greater odor detection rates on no odor trials for the strong cue compared to the weak cue. Importantly, this finding could not be explained by differences in total number of visual cue presentations or other task variables. Further, the difference in odor detection rate for the strong and weak cues during the supra-threshold conditioning trials predicted the difference in false odor detection during the no odor trials, suggesting that the prior formed between the strong cue and odor contributed to the false olfactory percepts. This demonstrates that false odor perception can be enhanced by the expectation of an olfactory stimulus in a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm. These findings could yield therapeutic insight into the mechanisms underlying pathological olfactory hallucinations.

items.title: NeuroMetaBench: Expert-curated benchmark for evaluating automated neuroimaging meta-analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychology, University of Texas at Austin
items.abstract: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis is widely used to generate hypotheses and interpret findings, reducing the time and effort required for manual literature searches and evidence curation. However, how closely these methods recover effortful expert-curated syntheses has not been established. We present NeuroMetaBench, an openly available benchmark linking expert curation records across stages of systematic review, from author-stated eligibility criteria and research-article inclusion decisions to individual analysis selections and meta-analysis-specific reference maps. The resource includes bibliographic records for 1,611 research-article inclusions across 17 quantitative review articles and candidate search pools for three. For nine review articles, it also provides analysis-level selections and coordinate data across 35 meta-analyses, documenting which reported results contributed to each meta-analysis and enabling reproducible construction of standardized reference maps. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating three established automated methods: Neurosynth, NeuroQuery, and NeuroVLM. Across the benchmark, automated maps generally showed limited to moderate spatial correspondence with expert-curated reference maps, with substantial variation across meta-analysis topics and characteristics. NeuroMetaBench provides an openly available, community-driven resource for evaluating established automated meta-analysis methods, and is well positioned to evaluate emerging LLM-based approaches to automated neuroimaging synthesis.

items.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
items.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how recurrent circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our results highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscillations at the stimulation frequency.

items.title: Tensor decomposition for data-driven analysis of OP-MEG: a feasibility study
items.corresponding_institution: Quantum Learning Labs, Department of Computer Science, University College London, London, United Kingdom
items.abstract: Optically Pumped Magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OP-MEG) enables flexible, close-to-scalp recordings unlocking access to new patient cohorts and naturalistic paradigms. The data collected during OP-MEG sessions is naturally multi-dimensional, often containing information across patients, trials, conditions, space, frequency and time which can be stored in tensors. Canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) is an unsupervised method that separates multidimensional data into components with linked spatial, spectral and temporal profiles. This allows neural responses to be characterised across brain regions, frequency and time simultaneously,without specifying these features in advance. This makes CPD well suited to OP-MEG data, where signals naturally vary across these dimensions. Here, we applied CPD to whole-brain, source-reconstructed OP-MEG data from three participants with epilepsy during a simple visuomotor task, modelling neural activity jointly across brain regions, frequency and time. We split these subject-specific tensors into event-related power decrease and increase (referred to as ERD and ERS for convenience) tensors so that a more interpretable and computationally efficient non-negative CPD variant could be applied. CPD paired with consensus clustering on spatio-spectral-temporal networks successfully identified cross-patient, simultaneous motor beta and visual alpha suppression. Permutation-based null distribution tests were used to exclude tensors that lacked significant low-rank structure. These findings demonstrate the applicability of tensor decompositions to electrophysiological data as the pipeline recovers canonical visuomotor responses without prespecifying region, band or latency.

items.title: Mutation induced disruption of domain coupling and interaction networks governs dysfunction of hDicer in recognizing pre-miRNA
items.abstract: Human Dicer (hDicer) is a multidomain RNase III enzyme central to RNA interference. Precise coordination between different domains in hDicer governs recognition and processing of double-stranded RNA substrate. While recent structural studies reveal distinct apo and dicing conformations, dynamics and energetics basis of hDicer function, particularly the effect of mutations in RNA recognition remains elusive. In this study, we investigate the mechanistic impact of two specific mutations in hDicer, A872T in platform domain and H1549Y in RIIIDa domain, in recognizing pre-miRNA. Our study shows that the wild-type RNA-bound complex exhibits a relatively confined conformational landscape, stable coordination between helicase and PAZ domains, and a persistent protein-RNA interaction network contributing to domain coupling. The mutant, A872T retains near-WT binding energetics but induces altered conformational sampling, domain coordination and long-range communication accompanied by selective redistribution of hDicer-pre-miRNA interaction networks. Conversely, H1549Y induces broader conformational heterogeneity, increased RNA exposure and redistribution of interdomain communication networks. Dynamic residue-network analysis identifies recurrent communication regions that connect mutation-associated perturbations with distal structural regions. This supports a mutation-specific mechanism, where the effect of local sequence alteration propagates through pre-existing intramolecular communication networks to alter domain coupling and RNA-interface organization without requiring global structural destabilization. A872T predominantly exhibits selective network rewiring with energetic compensation, whereas H1549Y produces broader communication and interaction-network redistribution accompanied by weaker energetic stabilization. Given the involvement of Dicer-dependent miRNA dysregulation in neurodegeneration and cancer, our findings provide a structural framework for understanding how domain-specific mutations may influence hDicer function and miRNA processing.

items.title: Structural basis for Cas2/3 recruitment and nuclease-to-helicase DNA handover in type I-F CRISPR-Cas
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Graduate School of Bioresource and Bioenvironmental Sciences, Kyushu University
items.abstract: Type I CRISPR-Cas systems couple RNA-guided target recognition to DNA degradation by a Cas3 nuclease-helicase. However, how initial nicking of the displaced non-target strand (NTS) at the active site of the Cas3 HD nuclease domain is coordinated with its subsequent loading into the helicase module remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the canonical type I-F surveillance complex (Csy) from Vibrio parahaemolyticus in DNA-unbound and DNA-bound states, together with two Csy-DNA-Cas2/3 structures consistent with states before and after initial NTS cleavage. Target DNA binding elongates the Csy complex and repositions the Cas8 helical bundle domain, creating a Cas2/3 recruitment platform involving Cas8 and Cas5. Cas2/3 captures a flexible NTS segment as a bulge at its HD nuclease active site, where an open RecA1 gate loop permits substrate access. Comparison of the two Cas2/3-bound structures suggests that, following initial nicking, the PAM-proximal NTS product disengages from the Cas8 helical bundle domain and is redirected into the helicase channel. Together with biochemical analyses, these structures provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how initial nicking is coupled to loading of the cleaved NTS into the helicase channel in type I CRISPR-Cas systems.

items.title: Contractile Centrin Filaments Mediate Mechanical Coupling of Cilia at the Basal Body
items.abstract: Centrin is a conserved protein that localizes to centrioles and basal bodies across eukaryotes, where it performs scaffolding and structural functions. In ciliates, centrin additionally assembles into patterned, cellular-scale networks required for ultrafast changes in cell shape. Across distantly related algae, centrin forms fibrillar structures that connect the basal bodies to one another and to the nucleus. These features suggest that centrin has cytoskeletal functions, generating and resisting mechanical forces, yet its functions in this context remain poorly understood. Here, we use expansion microscopy and centrin mutants with different network morphologies to study the function of centrin filaments in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Consistent with previous studies, centrin localizes to the basal bodies and transition zones, to the distal striated fiber, which connects the distal ends of the two basal bodies, and to filaments that extend from the basal bodies toward the nucleus, where they branch into a network that surrounds it. Using mutants of basal body proteins, we show that these centrin fibers assemble independently of basal bodies, which anchor and orient them. Centrin mutants have shorter cilia that regenerate more slowly, consistent with centrin's structural roles at the basal bodies and transition zones. Beyond these structural roles, centrin serves a mechanical function at the distal striated fiber. Mutants with structural defects in this centrin network show altered ciliary beat frequency and lack synchrony between the two cilia, resulting in impaired swimming. Moreover, the transition zone, the distal striated fiber, and the nucleus-basal body connectors each contract in response to calcium. Together, these results show that centrin assembles into basal body-associated networks that combine structural scaffolding with calcium-responsive contractility and force transmission. Our findings establish centrin as a bona fide cytoskeletal protein and provide insight into how a single protein can diversify to perform distinct structural and mechanical functions within the same cell.

items.title: IκBα loss impairs mitochondrial homeostasis and primes cells for senescence
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Protein Research, The University of Osaka
items.abstract: Inflammatory signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction are hallmarks of cellular senescence, yet how these processes are coordinated remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify I{kappa}B, a well-known inhibitor of NF-{kappa}B, as a regulatory factor that links mitochondrial homeostasis to stress-induced cell death and senescence. Knockdown (KD) of I{kappa}B did not by itself induce a fully established senescent state but instead generated a senescence-primed state characterized by cellular hypertrophy, reduced DNA synthesis, metabolic remodeling, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Time-course proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses revealed a selective reduction of mitochondrial inner membrane-associated proteins in I{kappa}B KD cells and attenuated early signaling responses to TNF stimulation, respectively. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further indicated that a smaller fraction of I{kappa}B KD cells was predicted to transition toward a pro-apoptotic state. Among canonical I{kappa}B family members, induction of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) was specific to I{kappa}B KD, even though mitochondrial dysfunction was more pronounced in I{kappa}B{beta} and I{kappa}B{varepsilon} KD. These findings suggest that I{kappa}B influences the balance between post-stress cellular senescence and cell death through mechanisms that include maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis.

items.title: Nonsense-mediated mRNA Decay Inhibition Triggers Immunogenicity by HLA Class I Immunopeptide Remodeling in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Cells
items.abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) is a post-transcriptional surveillance pathway that degrades aberrant transcripts harboring premature termination codons. Thereby, NMD also limits the abundance of transcripts encoding potentially immunogenic peptides. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of the NMD kinase SMG1 remodels the human leukocyte antigen class I (HLA-I) immunopeptidome and enhances immune recognition of H838 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Treatment with a SMG1 inhibitor (SMG1i) effectively perturbed NMD, as reflected by increased abundance of NMD-sensitive transcripts. To identify NMD inhibition-associated HLA-I peptides beyond the canonical proteome, long-read RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling were integrated to generate a cell-specific sequence database for immunopeptidomic analysis. Identified peptides were further evaluated using an extended metascore incorporating predicted HLA binding and proteasomal processing to define a high-confidence HLA-I peptide repertoire. Of the 2,728 peptides passing the 1% false discovery rate threshold, 48 were detected exclusively in SMG1i-treated samples. Of these, 32 fulfilled additional criteria for recurrence, peptide length, and predicted binding to the genotyped H838 HLA-I alleles. The observed changes in HLA-I-bound immunopeptides were not accompanied by an increase in global surface HLA-I abundance, suggesting remodeling of peptide composition rather than increased HLA-I presentation capacity. Exploratory allogeneic co-culture experiments showed SMG1i-induced IFN-{gamma} response in partially HLA-matched CD8 T-cells compared with an unmatched donor and increased expression of effector-associated genes. Together, these findings establish a cell-specific, proteogenomic, and HLA-informed framework for identifying SMG1i-associated HLA-I peptides in an NSCLC model and prioritizing candidates for peptide-specific functional validation.

items.title: Axon initial segment as an axonal lysosome trafficking control gate
items.corresponding_institution: School of Life Sciences, Southern University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Spatial subcellular distributions of lysosomes are intricately coupled with their functional heterogeneities, yet how neurons preferentially allocate distinct subtypes of lysosomes between the soma and axons remains largely unknown. Here, we discover that the axon initial segment (AIS) may function as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint by actively sorting lysosomes based on their functional states. Central to this checkpoint is MCF2L, a specific lysosome-associated protein enriched in AIS, that anchors clustered lysosomes at AIS via high-affinity binding to giant ankyrin-G (gAnkG, encoded by Ank3). Selective ablation of the MCF2L-gAnkG interaction accelerates disease progression in a mouse Parkinson's disease model. By clustering lysosomes, MCF2L restricts kinesin-mediated transport and regulates lysosomal positioning. In neurons, MCF2L-mediated lysosome clustering may act as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint, by which less acidic (e.g., impaired) lysosomes are retained in AIS and functionally intact lysosomes are released for transport. Thus, AIS may impart neurons with a unique mechanism for axonal lysosome compartmentalization and quality control.

items.title: Transposon-driven pervasive genome restructuring and regulatory evolution in early-diverging Holomycota
items.abstract: Early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi showcase major evolutionary transitions in the fungal kingdom, share features with other eukaryotic clades and bacteria, and include pathogens of significant concern. These lineages contain some of the most reduced and expanded genome architectures of the fungal kingdom and have adopted unique DNA methylation systems. Yet, the evolutionary trajectory of early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi remains poorly understood. A key driver is thought to be transposable elements, which shape genomic plasticity, organization and regulation. Here, we perform a comprehensive comparative analysis across the Holomycota to chart drivers of early fungal evolution. We demonstrate that contrasting transposon dynamics directly shape genomic diversity across these lineages, fueling extensive protein domain expansions through widespread co-option. This heterogeneous landscape is regulated by a multi-layered epigenetic network impacting chromatin configuration, and we reveal a distinct transcriptional activation role for adenine methylation over specific transposons. Beyond driving functional innovation, mobile elements serve as a source of regulatory diversification, providing transcription factor binding sites at key chromosomal features. Furthermore, synteny tracking uncovers multiple whole-genome duplication events across Mucoromycotina, where DNA transposons preferentially accumulate at duplication breakpoints and undergo rapid inactivation. Strikingly, we also show that horizontal transposon transfers frequently cross deep evolutionary boundaries, including cross-kingdom exchanges with protists. Together, our findings illuminate key drivers of genome architecture in non-Dikarya fungi and reshape our understanding of genome dynamics across the fungal kingdom.

items.title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
items.abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://igvf.catalog.org) Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog's utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease. Updated quarterly with open data and software, the IGVF Catalog provides a scalable resource for variant-to-function discovery.

items.title: Unsupervised tensor integration of hippocampal and colonic multi-omics reveals enteric neural signatures in cognitive aging
items.abstract: Background: Molecular changes in peripheral tissues may provide insights into cognitive aging, but identifying relevant genes without using behavioral outcomes for feature selection remains challenging. Results: We applied tensor decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction to publicly available hippocampal and colonic transcriptomic and promoter DNA methylation profiles from mice across five age groups. A tensor comprising tissue, molecular modality, age group, biological replicate, and gene dimensions was constructed using 16,080 shared genes. Higher-order singular value decomposition identified a component with a monotonic age pattern, shared tissue contributions, and opposing transcriptomic and methylation contributions. This component yielded 1,577 selected genes without using cognitive scores for feature selection. The corresponding colonic methylation score correlated with overall cognition (r=0.589; Benjamini--Hochberg-adjusted P=9.87 x10-7), although no significant associations remained after age adjustment. The selected genes were enriched for enteric neuronal and glial markers derived from a published single-cell atlas, with 5.10-fold and 4.65-fold enrichment, respectively. Comparison with the broadest available Boruta-selected gene set identified only 64 overlapping genes, leaving 1,513 genes selected exclusively by the tensor approach in this comparison. These remaining genes retained significant enrichment for synaptic processes and enteric neuronal and glial signatures using library-specific backgrounds. Conclusions: Unsupervised tensor integration recovered an aging-associated relationship between colonic methylation and cognition while identifying a largely distinct set of functionally coherent candidate genes. These findings complement supervised feature selection and provide candidates for investigating enteric neural involvement in cognitive aging, without establishing an age-independent association or a causal gut-to-brain mechanism.

items.title: The IGVF Data Portal: a repository for insights into genome function
items.abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) Consortium has utilized a wide variety of assays and computational methods to study how genomic variation impacts function. To support the collaborative efforts of labs within IGVF, and to share the results of these efforts, the IGVF Data Administration and Coordination Center (DACC) has developed a data portal (https://data.igvf.org/) that serves as the repository for all results from the IGVF Consortium and as the source of results that have been integrated into the IGVF knowledge graph. Data generated by the IGVF Consortium, which has reached over 240 terabytes as of November 2026, can be publicly accessed via web browser, or programmatically via API, as well as via agentic tools. Here, we provide a summary of the available IGVF data and an overview of the design of the IGVF Data Portal.

items.title: Lysosome Exocytosis Inhibition Impairs Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Cell Invasion
items.corresponding_institution: iNOVA4Health, NOVA Medical School, Faculdade de Ciências Médicas, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Campo dos Mártires da Pátria, 130, Lisboa 1169-056, Portugal
items.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women, with metastasis remaining the leading cause of mortality. Among BC molecular subtypes, triple-negative BC (TNBC) is the most aggressive, characterized by high metastatic potential and limited treatment options, underscoring the need for developing new therapeutic strategies. Cancer progression relies on the subversion of multiple cellular processes, among which lysosome exocytosis is described as a major driver of cell invasion. Indeed, lysosome exocytosis has been shown to play a role in extracellular matrix degradation and remodeling, which is particularly relevant to sustain cancer cell invasive capacity. In this study, we show that highly-invasive BC cell lines present increased levels of lysosome exocytosis when compared to non- or low-invasive ones. To investigate the functional effect of inhibiting this pathway on TNBC cell invasion, we used a genetic approach, by silencing RAB10 or a pharmacological strategy, using rosmarinic acid, and assessed invasive capacity. Both approaches significantly decreased lysosome exocytosis, measured as the release of the lysosome enzyme {beta}-hexosaminidase, and strongly impaired TNBC cell invasive capacity. Together, these findings highlight the potential of lysosome exocytosis as a therapeutic target to impair TNBC cell invasion, hindering BC progression, and improving patient prognosis.

items.title: A new thermophysiological model unifying heat balance theory and physiological feedback control: Framework, heat defence functions, and individualisation
items.abstract: Coded in Julia using ModelingToolkit, we developed a new computational model (TeMP) that calculates the emergent physiological responses to heat with and without physical activity (PA). Rooted in established physical and physiological principles, we detail the model framework, major novelties, and sources of individual variation. TeMP uses physical heat-transfer and heat-balance concepts to determine the rate of whole-body heat storage (S) over a given exposure period, based on the dynamic relationship between S, tissue temperature, and thermoeffector function. Each thermoeffector (skin blood flow, sweating, and ventilation) operates on independent feedback loops and is modelled based on afferent inputs from central and peripheral/skin tissue temperatures. All thermoeffectors use simple piecewise equations to determine the onset threshold, slope, and maximum functions, removing the need for a central error signal pervasive in alternative models. Skin blood flow is bounded by individual fitness level and is attenuated by PA, whereas sweating is more sensitive during PA due to heightened sympathetic activity. Minute ventilation is also bounded by individual fitness and is sensitive to body temperature and PA intensity, capturing the disproportionate increase in breathing rate at the ventilatory threshold. Thermoeffector functions are individualised for intrinsic characteristics, including heat acclimatisation, age, menstrual cycle phase, skin grafting, sympathetic blockade (i.e., spinal cord lesion), and severe energy restriction (i.e., anorexia nervosa). Finally, heart and rectal temperature are modelled independently and follow similar divergent patterns shown in empirical studies at rest and during PA.

items.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
items.abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices--signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set--into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time-frequency decomposition including the delta band (2-4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

items.title: Lipidomic Profiling of L1CAM+ Extracellular Vesicles in Parkinson's Disease
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) lacks minimally invasive biomarkers that reflect neuron-derived molecular alterations. Here, we performed a pilot study for untargeted Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS)-based lipidomics on serum total extracellular vesicles (tEVs) and L1CAM-enriched EVs (L1CAM+EVs) in patients with PD and healthy controls (n=10 per group; N=40). Partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) separated PD from control samples in both fractions L1CAM+EVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.879; tEVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.876), and distinguished L1CAM+EVs from tEVs within PD samples (R2Y = 0.999, Q2 = 0.925). In PD tEVs, triacylglycerols, fatty acids, phosphatidylcholines, sphingomyelins and phosphatidylserines were increased, and pathway analysis indicated enhanced conversion of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) to phosphatidylserine (PS). In contrast, PD L1CAM+EVs showed increased DG, LPA and PS with reduced LPC; pathway reconstruction indicated enhanced PE-PC-DG and LPC-PC flux with reduced de novo PC and SM synthesis. Within PD, L1CAM+EVs were depleted of multiple sphingomyelin species (e.g., SM 41:2;O3, SM 35:2;O3, SM 41:3;O3) and glycerophospholipids relative to tEVs, whereas SPB 18:0;O2 and FA 16:4 were relatively enriched. These findings indicate that L1CAM-enriched EVs carry a PD-associated lipid signature that is qualitatively distinct from that of controls, supporting their evaluation as a complementary source of neuron-related lipid biomarkers.

items.title: Needle in a haystack: Fluorescence-guided 3D targeting for FIB milling in high-pressure-frozen samples
items.abstract: Rare subcellular structures are difficult to retain during lamella preparation for cryo-electron tomography, particularly in high-pressure-frozen specimens. Here we introduce two complementary workflows for three-dimensional fluorescence-guided milling on a commercial cryo-focused ion beam-scanning electron microscope with integrated fluorescence imaging. Iterative fluorescence correlation uses repeated rounds of imaging and milling to refine the target position, whereas bidirectional fluorescence correlation images a lifted-out block from two orthogonal directions. We validated both by targeting centrosomes in waffle-frozen early Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, each of which occupy approximately 0.007% of the embryo volume. We recovered recognizable centrosomes in 83% and 67% of lamellae examined by transmission electron microscopy, respectively, compared with 25% using a refined, 2D-guided high-throughput SOLIST workflow, run as a benchmark. Neither method requires hardware modification or fluorescent fiducial beads. These workflows provide accessible strategies for targeting rare subcellular structures during lamella preparation, with or without a lift-out hardware.

items.title: Expression, Purification and Preliminary Analysis of REcTO4, an Engineered Chimeric PIN-Domain Endoribonuclease
items.abstract: REcTO4 (R4) is an engineered chimeric protein that combines the PIN endoribonuclease domain of Regnase-1 with the tandem zinc-finger (TZF) RNA-binding domain of tristetraprolin (TTP), designed to promote the targeted degradation of pro-inflammatory mRNAs. Recombinant production and purification of this bifunctional chimeric protein in soluble form presents substantial challenges, including the need to accommodate two structurally distinct functional domains that must fold in the bacterial cytoplasm, as well as the interaction of the TZF domain with endogenous RNA. Here, we describe the systematic expression, screening, optimization of purification procedures, and biochemical/biophysical characterization of recombinant GST-tagged R4. Among the five expression constructs designed, only the N-terminally GST-tagged construct yielded an appreciable amount of soluble, catalytically active protein in Escherichia coli. An optimized two-step purification protocol, combining GST affinity and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), yielded GST-R4 with a purity exceeding 95%. GST-R4 also co-purifies with endogenous bacterial RNA, forming high-molecular-weight complexes with apparent molecular mass of approximately 570 kDa by SEC. Endoribonuclease assay performed after affinity purification showed detectable RNA-cleavage activity. Preliminary cryo-EM micrographs reveal heterogeneous particles of approximately 10 nm, together with filamentous features consistent with assemblies of RNA-protein complexes, but intrinsic sample heterogeneity currently prevents 2D/3D reconstruction. This methodology reported here establishes an expression and purification workflow for GST-R4 and provides a foundation for structural and functional studies of this novel chimeric enzyme class engineered for pharmacological application.

items.title: The AAA+ ATPase RUVBL2 is a dual switch controlling invadosome formation and architecture
items.abstract: Metastatic dissemination requires tumour cells to degrade the extracellular matrix through invadosomes, actin-rich degradative structures whose architecture adapts to the microenvironment. Here we identify the AAA+ ATPase RUVBL2 as a dual regulator of invadosome biology. RUVBL2 is enriched in tumours and accumulates dynamically within rosette invadosomes together with the R2TP components. RUVBL2 depletion abolishes invadosome formation and matrix degradation, reverts invasive cells to a stress-fibre phenotype and suppresses activating Src phosphorylation. Conversely, RUVBL2 overexpression induces degradation-competent invadosomes in non-invasive cells. This pro-invasive function does not require RUVBL2 ATPase activity: pharmacological or genetic ATPase inactivation preserves punctate invadosomes and matrix degradation but selectively abolishes rosette architecture, which instead depends on ATPase-driven assembly of an R2TP-like scaffold. RUVBL2 protein is elevated in tumours; its transcript levels are increased at metastatic stages in m and associated with poor survival in several cancers. RUVBL2 therefore couples the Src-dependent initiation of invasion to the higher-order structural organisation of invadosomes.

items.title: CD133-dependent membrane organization shapes extracellular vesicle heterogeneity in triple-negative breast cancer
items.abstract: Extracellular vesicle (EV) heterogeneity is well established, but how distinct EV populations emerge from the same donor cell remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated plasma membrane organization as a potential contributor to EV molecular heterogeneity in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). CD133/PROM1 expression was associated with plasma membrane remodeling, including prominent protrusion formation, and with the redistribution of the EV-associated tetraspanin CD63 toward these domains. Quantitative immunogold electron microscopy revealed a disproportionate enrichment of CD63 labeling within protrusions following CD133 expression. This remodeling was accompanied by increased EV particle output and altered EV-associated marker signals. Single-particle analysis identified distinct CD133/CD63, CD133/CD63-, and CD133-/CD63 EV populations, demonstrating that CD133 and CD63 were not uniformly distributed across detected EVs. CD63 was detected more frequently in the CD133 than in the CD133- EV fraction, supporting an association between CD133 expression and EV marker heterogeneity. CD133 expression was also associated with changes in intracellular multivesicular body (MVB) density and size distribution, with different responses across the two TNBC cell models examined. Together, these findings suggest that plasma membrane organization may contribute to EV heterogeneity alongside context-dependent remodeling of intracellular MVB compartments. Rather than implicating CD133 in a single EV biogenesis pathway, our data highlight spatial membrane organization as a potential determinant of EV molecular diversity.

items.title: β-tubulin tyrosination tunes glutamylation and parasite motility in Trypanosoma brucei
items.abstract: Post-translational modifications of tubulin diversify microtubule function by generating distinct molecular states collectively known as the tubulin code. Whereas the reversible tyrosination cycle is a conserved feature of -tubulin throughout eukaryotes, in trypanosomatid parasites, {beta}-tubulin also carries a genetically encoded C-terminal tyrosine, which is subjected to detyrosination and whose biological role remains unknown. Here, we show that {beta}-tubulin tyrosination is rare across eukaryotes but highly conserved across trypanosomatids. Using genome editing to uncouple the tyrosination states of - and {beta}-tubulin in Trypanosoma brucei, we demonstrate that the {beta}-tubulin C-terminal tyrosine independently contributes to the regulation of microtubule glutamylation. Rather than depending on - or {beta}-tubulin alone, glutamylation levels reflect the combined tyrosination states of both subunits. Strikingly, either increasing or reducing {beta}-tubulin tyrosination produces opposing changes in parasite morphometry, single-cell motility and collective migration. Together, these findings establish {beta}-tubulin (de)tyrosination as an evolutionarily conserved component of the trypanosomatid tubulin code that contributes to microtubule regulation and function in T. brucei, extending the significance of tubulin tyrosination beyond the canonical -tubulin tyrosination cycle.

items.title: Predicting Cell Movement for Low-Frame-Rate Tracking
items.abstract: Automated cell tracking is widely used to quantify cellular behavior and typically involves two steps: identifying cells in each observation and linking corresponding cells across observations. This paper focuses on the linking problem under low-frame-rate imaging. Low-frame-rate imaging mitigates photobleaching and phototoxicity and enables long term observations, but larger cell displacements make spatial proximity less reliable and increase ambiguity among candidate links. We investigate whether cell images contain information about future movement direction that can provide an additional cue for cell linking. We systematically evaluate the impact of image-patch configurations, direction representations, and deep-learning architectures for movement-direction prediction accuracy. Moreover, we incorporate the predicted directions into a Linear Assignment Problem (LAP)-based linking method and evaluate linking performance across four cell lines and multiple temporal gaps. Our results show that movement-direction information can improve cell linking by 2.7 to 5.7 percentage points over the distance-only LAP baseline, depending on the cell line, at a two-hour interval between frames. Among the evaluated configurations, a CNN-LSTM with a class-based direction representation provides the largest improvement (4.1 percentage points on average) over the distance-only LAP baseline. These results show that cell images provide a cue for cell linking that spatial proximity alone does not capture.

items.title: The cell cycle controls centrosome growth by regulating the dynamics of two distinct scaffolds
items.corresponding_institution: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology
items.abstract: Centrosomes comprise a pair of centrioles that organise a surrounding pericentriolar material (PCM) that usually grows as cells prepare to enter mitosis, stops growing during mitosis, and then shrinks as cells exit mitosis. In most models of centrosome growth, the PCM stops growing because cells run out of a limiting component. Using experiments and mathematical modelling in the early Drosophila embryo, we show that the embryonic cell cycle oscillator (CCO) can generate these centrosome growth kinetics without relying on the depletion of a limiting component. At the start of each cycle centrioles assemble two dynamic and interconnected PCM scaffolds comprising Spd-2/CEP192 and Cnn/CDK5RAP2. As embryos approach mitosis, rising CCO activity destabilises the Spd-2 scaffold, slowing centrosome growth, but stabilises the Cnn scaffold, locking it into a low-dynamic state. At the end of mitosis CCO activity drops, triggering rapid Cnn scaffold disassembly. Thus, the CCO drives centrosome growth dynamics by regulating the stability of two interconnected PCM scaffolds.

items.title: Cortical neurons accumulate point mutations at similar rates in mice and humans
items.abstract: Across vertebrate species, it has long been known that germline mutation rates per year are inversely proportional to reproductive ages. A similar pattern was recently reported in mammals for mutations in colonic epithelium, leading to speculation that this inter-species scaling may apply to many cell types. We tested whether a similar relationship holds in postmitotic cells, by estimating point mutation rates in mouse cortical neurons from PacBio HiFi circular consensus sequencing data. Our analysis revealed a significant effect of age on the number of point mutations, of 25.9 mutations per diploid genome per year (95% CI: [17.7, 34.1]). This rate is comparable to the one reported for human neurons, indicating that somatic rates need not scale with lifespan. Our findings further demonstrate that a readily available sequencing method can be used to reliably identify somatic mutations at single-cell resolution.

items.title: Genomic Characterisation of the Irish Traditional BoRiabhach Cattle Breed
items.abstract: The BoRiabhach is a highly endangered traditional landrace cattle breed in Ireland with a culturally significant history. The Irish Gaelic word "riabhach" means "streaked", "striped", or "brindled", and a distinctive brindle coat colour pattern is characteristic of the BoRiabhach breed. The breed had declined to about 20 animals by 2016 and has no systematic pedigree. Despite conservation efforts that have increased the population to an estimated 70 animals, the breed remains one of Europe's most critically endangered livestock genetic resources. We present the first genomic characterisation of the BoRiabhach breed, using Illumina BovineSNP50 genotypes of 84 BoRiabhach animals and 688 cattle from 28 European comparator breeds. Using model-based clustering, we identified a BoRiabhach-specific ancestry component. Only 28 animals carried more than 50% of this component, which we term "high-BRBH"; the remaining 56 showed extensive introgression, chiefly from Limousin and Holstein, which explains the breed's high observed heterozygosity. Phylogenetic analysis placed the high-BRBH cohort with British Shorthorn and Lincoln Red within a British-Irish clade, distinct from Kerry and Dexter, and recovered a Limousin-to-BoRiabhach migration edge. This high-BRBH core group exhibited the lowest effective population size (Ne) of any adequately sampled breed and consists of closely related animals: 34% of pairs within the core were second-degree relatives or closer. Conservation of the BoRiabhach must therefore balance breed distinctiveness with genetic diversity. We recommend genotyping all extant animals, recording genomic ancestry at registration, managing mating based on genomic relatedness as well as ancestry, and cryopreserving germplasm from the high-BRBH core population.

items.title: Identification of eukaryotes as a bycatch in global microbiome data
items.abstract: Eukaryotes shape microbiomes as macroscopic hosts, microscopic community members, and food sources, yet the diversity and ecological significance of microbial eukaryotes remain poorly resolved. Here, we present metaEukaryome, an organelle genome-centered framework for detection of eukaryotes in metagenomic data that leverages mitochondrial and plastid sequences as robust signatures of presence. Applying metaEukaryome to 75,727 metagenomic samples collected across the globe reveals strong environment-specific patterns in the prevalence of detected eukaryotes. Integrating eukaryotic and prokaryotic profiles further reveals recurrent cross-domain co-occurrence and symbiosis in the human gut. In particular, Blastocystis is associated with metabolically reduced, uncultured bacterial clades, including Candidatus Borkfalkia and CAG-345, whose DNA and RNA are detected in a Blastocystis culture previously reported as axenic. Their complementary metabolic repertoires further support a candidate symbiotic relationship. These findings imply that more novel (endo-)symbionts of gut protists can be discovered by reanalysing existing data.

items.title: Plasma electrolyte changes can modulate post-repolarisation refractoriness in the human atrium
items.abstract: Changes in plasma Na+, K+ and Ca2+ levels are common in patients with chronic kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, or in those taking certain medications, and may promote atrial fibrillation or impair drug-induced cardioversion. Post-repolarisation refractoriness (PRR) is an established mechanism by which antiarrhythmic drugs suppress tachyarrhythmias. We investigated how changes in extracellular Na+, K+ and Ca2+ concentrations ([Na+]o, [K+]o, [Ca2+]o) modulate ionic currents and PRR in healthy and fibrotic human atrial tissue. We used a multi-scale computational framework comprising an isolated atrial myocyte, a one-dimensional atrial tissue strand, and a virtual cohort of 14 left atrial digital twins, combined with Gaussian process emulators and variance-based global sensitivity analysis. Changes in [K+]o strongly modulated PRR by altering the inward rectifier K+ current (IK1), shifting the resting potential and thereby regulating Na+-current availability. In contrast, [Na+]o had only a weak effect on PRR, mediated primarily through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and [Ca2+]o had a negligible effect. Tissue PRR was more sensitive to electrolyte changes than myocyte PRR, reflecting electrolyte-dependent alterations in the safety factor for action potential propagation. Changes in [K+]o also substantially affected arrhythmia vulnerability, increasing inducibility and prolonging rhythm disturbances. We conclude that extracellular K+ is the principal plasma electrolyte determinant of atrial PRR and arrhythmia burden, acting primarily through IK1. Monitoring and maintaining serum K+ within the normal range may be important for managing atrial arrhythmia risk.

items.title: Caspase-7 cleavage repurposes AAK1 to suppress mRNA decay and promote tolerance to anti-tubulin agents
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular Medicine, Long School of Medicine, The University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX 78229, USA; Current address: Department of He
items.abstract: Prolonged mitotic arrest imposed by anti-tubulin chemotherapy suppresses transcription, making mRNA preservation critical for tumor-cell survival. Here, we identify an unexpected kinase-repurposing mechanism that sustains this adaptation. A kinome-wide screen revealed clathrin-adaptor kinase AAK1 as a determinant of taxane tolerance. During mitotic arrest, CDK1 phosphorylates AAK1 at T389 to enhance catalytic activity, while caspase-7 cleaves AAK1 at D767, removing a clathrin-binding domain. These modifications produce a cleaved fragment with reduced clathrin association and increased association with CCR4-NOT, suppressing mRNA decay and maintaining glycolytic gene expression. Mutant-rescues establish that both phosphorylation and cleavage contribute to cancer-cell survival during paclitaxel-induced arrest. A clinical-stage AAK1 inhibitor developed for neuropathic pain sensitized cancer cells to paclitaxel. Together, these findings reveal how coordinated phosphorylation and proteolysis repurpose a trafficking kinase to maintain mRNA stability, uncovering an unexpected tolerance-promoting function of caspase cleavage and a therapeutically actionable vulnerability of chemotherapy-arrested cancer cells.

items.title: Targeting MondoA Sensitizes B-ALL Cells to Asparaginase and Reveals Glutathione-Associated Protection
items.abstract: Background: L-Asparaginase (ASNase) is central to acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) therapy, but resistance and long-term cytotoxic effects remain challenging. We investigated whether MondoA (MLXIP) modulates ASNase sensitivity. Methods: Viability and apoptosis were assessed in CRISPR-Cas9-generated MondoA-knockout (MKO), MondoA-overexpressing (MOE), and Cas9-only control (WT) Nalm6 B-ALL cells following ASNase exposure or glutamine depletion. Omics, ChIP-seq, and patient-RNA-seq examined MondoA-ASNS associations. Results: MondoA deficiency was associated with reduced ASNS mRNA and protein abundance. MYC binding to the ASNS promoter was reduced in MKO cells, suggesting an indirect transcriptional link. MondoA and ASNS expression correlated in patient samples, particularly in T-ALL (r = 0.769). MKO cells showed increased ASNase, but not doxorubicin or vincristine, sensitivity. Glutamine withdrawal during ASNase treatment further reduced viability. GSH-associated protection was strongest in biallelic MKO2. Conclusion: MondoA status was associated with ASNS abundance and ASNase response, warranting further investigation of these processes as candidate determinants of ASNase sensitivity.

items.title: NADH regulation shapes competing acetate flux responses in Escherichia coli: kinetic modelling of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and acetate production
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Melbourne - Parkville Campus
items.abstract: Overflow metabolism occurs when cells divert carbon towards fermentative products despite oxygen availability. In rapidly growing Escherichia coli, it is primarily characterised by acetate secretion. An elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio has been proposed to contribute to this behaviour, but the mechanisms linking redox imbalance to acetate production remain unclear. We developed a kinetic model linking pyruvate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and acetate formation to examine how cofactor availability and NADH-mediated enzyme regulation influence carbon partitioning. The model combines thermodynamically consistent reversible rate laws with NADH inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and citrate synthase, and was calibrated using Bayesian inference to account for parameter uncertainty. We examined steady-state responses to changes in the target NADH/NAD+ ratio and the total NAD(H) pool size. With both inhibitory interactions included, lowering the target redox ratio increased acetate-producing flux, contrary to the experimentally observed reduction in acetate secretion. Substantially attenuating the effective NADH response of PDH recovered the experimental direction of this response. Additionally, to reproduce the observed reduction in acetate secretion following NAD(H)-pool expansion, a weak but non-zero PDH response was required. These findings suggest that cofactor-dependent kinetics and NADH-mediated regulation can jointly contribute to carbon redistribution between the TCA cycle and acetate production. Within this restricted model, whether a more reduced redox state promotes acetate-producing flux depends critically on the effective NADH sensitivity of PDH.

items.title: Model evaluation metrics of Virtual Cell Challenge 2026
items.corresponding_institution: Arc Institute, Palo Alto, CA, USA
items.abstract: Virtual cell models aim to predict the effects of genetic, environmental, chemical and other perturbations in silico, reducing the dependency on complex and costly experiments. The Virtual Cell Challenge 2026 motivates the field toward this goal, tasking models with zero-shot prediction of the transcriptional responses to CRISPRi knockdowns in six human cell lines. The faithfulness of a model to the experiment is assessed by metrics that compare its predictions with the real data, and designing such metrics is not trivial. We developed the metrics of the 2026 Challenge around three principles: a metric should (i) reflect the biological information extracted from experiments, (ii) be calibrated on a repeat of the experiment, and (iii) resist shortcut solutions that raise the score without predicting the response. Here we present the six resulting metrics, the reasoning behind each of them, and their evaluations on the Challenge data. Two of the metrics compare the pseudobulk expression profiles of predicted and measured cells, while four assess the genes that respond to each perturbation, the central readout of a Perturb-seq experiment. The metrics are implemented in cell-eval2, an open-source Python package. On the Challenge data, all six metrics score a repeat of the experiment above the mean baseline, and the shortcut solutions that the metrics of the 2025 Challenge left open can no longer raise the score. The new metrics are therefore more robust than the previous ones.

items.title: Substitution and Concomitant Distractor Intrusions Reveal Different Neural Dynamics of Temporal Selection
items.abstract: Selective attention requires target identification and exclusion of irrelevant information. We distinguished substitution and concomitant distractor intrusions in 29 adults performing rapid serial visual presentation with uncertain target number. Substitution reports, in which only the distractor was reported, showed an attenuated and delayed N2 posterior contralateral (N2pc) component and a smaller P3b; intrusion probability decreased with target-distractor numerical distance. Concomitant reports included both identities without reliable differences in measured averaged event-related potentials from correct reports of the same sequence. However, target-first concomitant reports were distinguishable through distributed activity and showed reduced left-frontal power, predominantly in theta. Comparisons with correct single- and dual-target reports indicated that reporting two identities did not simply reproduce genuine two-target processing. These findings distinguish processing profiles of substitution and concomitant intrusions and extend temporal-selection accounts from attentional engagement to subsequent regulation of which processed identities enter report.

items.title: Reduced bushy cell firing limits binaural coding after cochlear synaptopathy
items.abstract: Listeners can experience difficulties with spatial hearing and speech understanding in complex acoustic environments despite near-normal hearing thresholds. Cochlear synaptopathy, which reduces auditory nerve input without elevating thresholds, is one candidate mechanism, but how this peripheral deafferentation disrupts binaural processing remains unclear. We adapted a physiologically constrained computational model incorporating the auditory periphery, spherical and globular bushy cells of the cochlear nucleus and the lateral superior olive (LSO) to examine the separate and combined effects of reduced afferent input and degraded spike timing. Synaptopathy was modeled as loss of auditory nerve inputs to bushy cells, whereas central myelin dysfunction was modeled as increased temporal jitter in bushy cell outputs. Loss of auditory nerve input substantially reduced bushy cell firing rates without degrading phase locking. Despite this preserved temporal precision, binaural tuning in the LSO declined disproportionately, where moderate afferent loss produced substantial reductions in sensitivity to interaural envelope phase differences. In contrast, temporal jitter preserved bushy cell firing rates but degraded phase locking and binaural tuning. Selective loss of input to excitatory versus inhibitory pathways produced opposite changes in overall LSO firing rate, yet both reduced binaural interaction. These results identify two mechanistically distinct routes to impaired binaural coding: too few precisely timed spikes, and a sufficient number of spikes arriving with inadequate temporal precision. These results predict that correcting myelin-related timing deficits alone would leave substantial binaural coding impairment when cochlear deafferentation persists, motivating interventions that address both diminished afferent drive and impaired transmission.

items.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
items.corresponding_institution: IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Beijing Normal University
items.abstract: Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

items.title: Computational model for Rumination as Self-Supervised Learning in a World Model
items.abstract: Rumination is a cognitive process characterized by repetitive negative thoughts that persist even in the absence of external threats. Although excessive rumination is associated with stress-related mental disorders, the computational mechanisms underlying its persistence and its impact on threat perception remain unclear. Here, we propose a computational framework in which rumination emerges from recursive learning within a world model. Inspired by the social defeat stress (SDS) paradigm in mice, our model assumes that direct experiences of social defeat first establish beliefs about the threat posed by an aggressor. These beliefs subsequently generate internally simulated experiences, which are repeatedly used to update the beliefs themselves. We investigated how this recursive process reshapes threat perception by allowing the rumination gain, a learning rate controlling internal belief updating, to take both positive and negative values. Through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis, we found that positive gains did not simply reinforce acquired threat beliefs, while negative gains did not simply erase them. Instead, both positive and negative gains could generate markedly divergent threat perceptions, with some simulated individuals perceiving severe threats and others perceiving almost none, despite identical initial beliefs and external experiences. These outcomes qualitatively resemble the coexistence of stress-susceptible and resilient mice following SDS. Our findings suggest that rumination is not merely a repetition of past experiences but a self-referential learning process that can transform identical stressful experiences into fundamentally different perceptions of threat.

items.title: Voluntary control of human motor units is more flexible in facial than limb muscles
items.abstract: Facial expressions require different motor circuits than those controlling the limbs. How the motor system uses flexible neural control across muscles innervated by the brainstem versus the spinal cord is unclear. Using intramuscular and surface electromyography in human participants performing low-effort, sustained voluntary contractions, we show that brainstem motor units function with more features of flexible control compared to motor units in several spinally innervated muscles. Individual motor units recorded from the frontalis muscle (brainstem-innervated) used a wider range of regular and irregular firing rates, reflecting both greater independence and higher input sensitivity than spinal-innervated motor units. When assessing motor unit pairs, we again found that brainstem control relied more heavily on features corresponding to independent inputs relative to spinal control. Voluntary control of brainstem-innervated muscle therefore used more flexible neural strategies than the control of upper and lower limb muscles we tested. These findings support an anatomical hypothesis for adaptive neural control, in which the degree of independent motor unit activation is constrained by how muscles are accessed across cortex.

items.title: Concurrent neuronal activity gates persistent dendritic spine shrinkage during mGluR-induced long-term depression
items.abstract: Synaptic plasticity is a fundamental mechanism underlying learning and memory. Most excitatory synapses reside on dendritic spines, which undergo both functional and structural changes. These two forms of plasticity are typically tightly coupled: spines enlarge during synaptic strengthening (long-term potentiation, LTP) and shrink during synaptic weakening (long-term depression, LTD). While this coupling is well established for NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent LTD, there are conflicting reports concerning whether spine shrinkage is coupled with metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD. To investigate the source of these conflicting results, we induced mGluR-LTD with the mGluR1/5 agonist DHPG in organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures and monitored changes in spine morphology and calcium transients in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing DsRed2 and GCaMP6. We found that mGluR activation is accompanied by long-term spine shrinkage only under conditions of elevated hippocampal neuronal activity. This form of plasticity, mGluR-induced neuronal activity-dependent structural LTD (MIND-sLTD), requires mGluR1/5 activation and de novo protein synthesis, but not NMDAR signaling. Persistent structural changes occur only when neuronal activity coincides temporally with mGluR activation. MIND-sLTD also occurs at individual synapses: mGluR activation induces persistent single-spine shrinkage only when synchronized with two-photon glutamate uncaging, independently of NMDARs. These findings identify a novel form of structural plasticity and suggest a coincidence-detection mechanism that integrates mGluR signaling with synaptic activity to consolidate long-term spine remodeling.

items.title: Structural basis for assembly of human cN1A filaments
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomolecular Chemistry, Institute for Molecules and Materials, Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands
items.abstract: Human cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of AMP to adenosine, is a prominent autoantigen in the progressive myopathy inclusion body myositis (IBM). Detection of anti-cN1A autoantibodies is a supportive criterion for IBM diagnosis, and mice immunized actively or passively with cN1A develop an IBM phenotype. However, how cN1A breaks immunotolerance is not yet known. Despite its clinical significance, the subcellular localization of cN1A is not well understood, and its structure has not been determined. Here, we show that human cN1A is most highly expressed in type 2 myofibers and tends to localize near the periphery of muscle fibers, but is either weakly expressed or undetectable in commonly used human cell lines. Ectopic expression of cN1A in such cells resulted in spontaneous assembly of cN1A into filamentous structures strikingly similar to metabolic filaments formed by the nucleotide biosynthesis enzymes IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH) and CTP synthase (CTPS). However, cN1A filaments did not co-localize with IMPDH or CTPS filaments and were not responsive to compounds that induce IMPDH and CTPS assembly. Negative stain electron microscopy (EM) showed that purified recombinant cN1A protein spontaneously polymerizes, suggesting filament assembly in cells is driven by intrinsic properties of cN1A. We then determined the structure of the cN1A filament by cryo-EM, which revealed that cN1A monomers assemble end-on-end into a polar helical filament and allowed us to identify contacts mediating filament assembly. Structure-guided mutations designed to abolish filament assembly prevented cN1A filament formation in cells, establishing the structural basis for cN1A filament assembly.

items.title: Interaction of yeast Vps13 with the calcium binding proteins Cdc31 and calmodulin
items.abstract: Vps13 is a member of the bridge-like lipid transfer protein superfamily involved in transport of lipids between different intracellular membranes. In yeast, deletion of VPS13 exhibits several distinct phenotypes due to preventing interorganelle lipid transfer between many different organelles. Vps13 shuttles lipids through a long hydrophobic channel, but how this activity is regulated in the cell is not yet understood. Studies in yeast and human cells have implicated small calcium-binding proteins, Cdc31 in yeast and calmodulin in mammalian cells, as potential regulators of Vps13 activity. This report identifies the binding site on Vps13 for Cdc31, the yeast ortholog of centrin. The yeast calmodulin protein Cmd1 binds Vps13 through the same site and separate Cmd1-Vps13 and Cdc31-Vps13 complexes co-exist in vivo. Association of Cmd1 with Vps13, but not Cdc31, is sensitive to the presence of Ca2+. A mutant of VPS13 that is unable to interact with either Cdc31 or Cmd1 is specifically defective in mitochondrial homeostasis and endoplasmic-reticulum (ER)-phagy, indicating that Vps13 binding to Cdc31 and/or Cmd1 is important for a subset of VPS13 functions.

items.title: A stop codon shared by all Gyps vultures, including the three Critically Endangered species of South Asia, lies in a coding exon of the bird gene CYP2C45
items.abstract: Veterinary diclofenac devastated three South Asian Gyps vultures, but the basis of their sensitivity is unclear. A stop codon reported in a Cape vulture P450 gene, described as CYP2C19 in a retained intron, was re-examined with public data: 45 genome assemblies, raw reads of seven Gyps birds and a liver transcriptome. The gene is the bird CYP2C45, without a one-to-one human orthologue. The stop (codon 338, CGA[->]TGA) lies in coding exon 7; the intron is spliced normally, the mRNA carries the stop, and the truncated protein lacks the haem-binding cysteine. The stop was found in all eight living Gyps species, homozygous wherever testable, and in none of 27 other raptors, including two killed by diclofenac. It arose once, 1.5-10.6 million years ago on the Gyps stem, and the gene has since evolved near-neutrally. This genus-wide loss marks Gyps vulnerability but cannot explain diclofenac deaths in other raptors.

items.title: Transpiling reproducibility: Multi-language implementation for the St. Nicolas House Analysis algorithm using Fusion
items.abstract: The integration of tools written in different programming languages is common in bioinformatics pipelines. When extending these tools, developers are required to either manually port the code or use wrapper libraries, which incurs a substantial "translation tax" on developer time. Transpilers have emerged as a potential solution, enabling the generation of algorithm implementations in multiple languages from a single source code base. However, it remains essential to establish whether transpiled code preserves both functional correctness and stochastic reproducibility across language ecosystems. In this case study, we investigated whether the Fusion language and its fut transpiler could produce functionally identical, stochastically reproducible, and high-performing code for the St. Nicolas House Analysis (SNHA) algorithm across multiple target languages. The SNHA algorithm was implemented once in Fusion and transpiled to nine target programming languages. The generated code was evaluated against reference R, Python, and Julia implementations using the clinical birthwt dataset and a 26-variable synthetic benchmark dataset evaluated over 1,000 bootstrap iterations. All nine transpiled outputs produced identical network structures to the original R implementation. With the deterministic Xorshift*64 pseudo-random number generator integrated into the algorithm, all languages generated identical bootstrapped datasets and adjacency matrices. Runtimes and memory usage spanned more than two orders of magnitude: the transpiled Python implementation achieved an 8.5-fold speedup and an 8.8-fold reduction in peak memory relative to reference Python, while compiled targets (C, C++) achieved speedups exceeding 160-fold and memory reductions up to 36-fold. These findings demonstrate that modern transpilers can eliminate cross-ecosystem translation tax while guaranteeing cross-language reproducibility in computational biology.

items.title: How predictable is an individual's DNA methylation?
items.abstract: DNA methylation is largely shared among individuals of the same cell type, yet at specific genomic sites it differs substantially between individuals. Methods that predict methylation are usually evaluated by their accuracy over all sites. Because methylation at most sites is shared, this accuracy cannot show whether a method predicts an individual's methylation where individuals differ. We present individual-level methylation prediction at sites where individuals differ as a new challenge. Given the reference genome sequence, the methylation of other individuals of the same cell type, and measurements at some sites of a target individual, but not the individual's genotype, the task is to predict the target individual's methylation class (unmethylated, intermediate, or methylated) at the remaining sites. We evaluate predictions separately at sites with low and high variation across individuals. We compare four approaches: the average of other individuals, a sequence model (the DNA language model Nucleotide Transformer) fine-tuned on other individuals' methylation, the same model further fine-tuned on the target individual's measurements, and a local class-average approach using the target individual's nearby training-site class labels. Across 32 individuals from six human cell types, the average of other individuals matched or slightly exceeded both sequence models at sites with low variation among individuals. At the most variable sites, the average of other individuals performed worse than a random predictor that assigns classes at the observed class frequencies, whereas both sequence models performed substantially better than the average. Both sequence models also achieved higher mean weighted F1 than the local class-average approach. Fine-tuning on the target individual's measurements improved predictions more inside regions where other individuals show bimodal methylation (a mix of methylated and unmethylated DNA molecules within one sample) than outside them. Among the most variable sites, it also improved predictions at CpG islands for 25 of the 32 individuals. We conclude that individual-level methylation prediction is a distinct problem that is particularly challenging at sites where individuals differ, and that the benefit of an individual's own measurements is concentrated in genomic contexts identifiable from other individuals' methylation and genomic annotations.

items.title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model
items.abstract: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.

items.title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
items.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn representations from DNA sequence, although their usefulness for variant classification depends on the architecture and downstream evaluation procedure. We compared six genomic foundation models using 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants from ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD)-associated genes, with 4,866 variants assigned to training and 2,094 to held-out testing.
