The analyses included frozen alternate-minus-reference embeddings at 101, 201 and 501 bp, supervised adaptation at 101 bp, and gene-held-out downstream classifier training. GPN-Star V100 and AlphaGenome Atlas AVI were evaluated separately using their native scores. At 101 bp, frozen Evo2 achieved the highest discrimination among the six foundation models (MCC 0.644; AUROC 0.879; AUPRC 0.818). Supervised adaptation increased MCC for three architectures and reduced it for the remaining three. Extending sequence context to 501 bp improved all three primary metrics in five of six frozen architectures, with Evo2 reaching an MCC of 0.864, AUROC of 0.964 and AUPRC of 0.952. Evo2 also led the frozen gene-held-out readouts (pooled MCC 0.641; AUROC 0.852; AUPRC 0.789). GPN-Star V100 and AVI achieved MCC values of 0.929 and 0.938, respectively, using distinct biological inputs and scoring procedures. The number of variants misclassified across all evaluated configurations decreased from five under the original 101-bp readouts to one after including longer contexts and native scores. An exploratory HGVS-category control identified substantial annotation-associated structure in the benchmark labels. The findings characterize classification performance against aggregate ClinVar labels within LGMD-associated genes. Disease-specific pathogenicity and clinical diagnostic utility remain untested.

items.title: Modeling Host-Virus Interactions of Avian Corona Virus Reveals Cytokine Feedback as a driver of Strain-Specific Immune Response
items.corresponding_institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Kolkata
items.abstract: The interplay between RNA viral dynamics and innate immunity remains poorly understood, mainly because RNA viruses trigger highly nonlinear cytokine responses. We address this using infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a major poultry pathogen, as a model system. We developed a set of mathematical models and compared those with experimental data from two IBV strains infecting chicken macrophages.By model fitting and supervised Machine Learning we reveal that positive feedback in interferon- production is essential to reproduce the dynamics of one IBV strain but likely absent in the other. We further provide strain-specific estimations of key parameters such as infection rates, production and decay rates of virus and cytokine levels. Notably, different strains produced distinctive cytokine profiles, highlighting feedback as a key determinant of strain-specific immune signatures. Our results establish a quantitative framework for dissecting host-virus interactions and uncover cytokine feedback as a generic yet underappreciated feature in models of RNA virus kinetics.

items.title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
items.corresponding_institution: Oxford Centre for Integrative Neuroimaging, Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Oxford, UK
items.abstract: Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44\% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

items.title: Shared and context-dependent cortico-striatal-cerebellar organization of temporal prediction
items.abstract: Temporal prediction is thought to draw on two subcortical structures: the basal ganglia for the periodic beat, and the cerebellum for the aperiodic interval. Lesion, imaging and electrophysiological studies converge on this division, yet each tests it within a single modality and task, leaving its generality unknown. We developed a battery of timing tasks for multi-task fMRI, densely sampling 31 non-clinical adults in every combination of temporal structure, sensory modality and task. Encoding engaged the same cortico-striatal-cerebellar architecture throughout. Within it, the dorsal striatum was uniquely selective for the production task. Pooled across tasks, it responded more to auditory beat than interval sequences, whereas the cerebellum did not distinguish them. Yet, removing regularity did not lower that response: the preference is for the beat, not for predictability. Temporal prediction therefore draws on a shared architecture whose striatal node is context-dependent: tuned to periodic time, and to time turned into action.

items.title: Modified Synchronization Modulation Electric Field attenuates acute brain injury and improves neurological outcomes following stroke induced by transient middle cerebral artery occlusion in rats
items.abstract: Cerebral ischemia disrupts energy-dependent ion transport and causes acute brain injury. The synchronization modulation electric field (SMEF) platform was developed to support Na+/K+-ATPase function under conditions of limited ATP availability and has shown protective effects in renal ischemia models. We investigated whether cerebral cortical application of third-generation SMEF attenuates cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) for 120 min, with or without SMEF treatment during ischemia. At 24 h after reperfusion, we assessed body-weight change, neurological deficits, open-field locomotor activity, cerebral infarct volume using 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining, hemispheric swelling, and cortical and striatal histopathology. Western blot analysis was performed to measure Na+/K+-ATPase 1, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-{kappa}B) p65 protein abundance. Compared with untreated MCAO rats, SMEF-treated rats exhibited significantly less body-weight loss, lower neurological deficit scores, greater total distance traveled, smaller edema-corrected infarct volumes and percentages, and lower cortical and striatal injury scores. SMEF also shifted Na+/K+-ATPase 1, GFAP, and NF-{kappa}B p65 protein abundance toward sham levels. These findings support an acute protective effect of SMEF following transient MCAO. Further studies should assess Na+/K+-ATPase activity and longer-term functional, histological, and molecular outcomes.

items.title: VisioWell, an all-in-one high-throughput platform to study haematopoietic cells division
items.abstract: Live-cell imaging has the potential to unravel crucial parameters for haematopoietic normal and leukaemic stem and progenitor cells. Yet, this technology requires a combination of technical and analytical skill sets that can be difficult to find in a traditional haematology lab. We present VisioWell, an all-in-one experimental platform specifically designed to measure the early division dynamics of blood stem and progenitor cells, from a simple brightfield long-term acquisition. We combined a simple custom-made microwell array to trap thousands of individual cells with a powerful semi-automatic analytical pipeline, able to segment, correct, and retrieve the division times for the first three sets of divisions. We validated VisioWell with primary cells from human cord blood and with a cellular model of myeloid leukaemia, revealing that CDK4/6 inhibition induces an increase in asynchronous division. By lowering the technical and analytical barriers to live-cell imaging, VisioWell makes label-free, non-destructive analysis of division dynamics accessible to any haematology lab, while preserving cells for downstream fate and functional readouts.

items.title: Local macrophage and cDC1 cooperation in the liver drives T-cell immune surveillance against pioneering metastatic cancer cells.
items.abstract: The liver is one of the most frequent sites for hematogenous metastasis across different types of cancer, but how the liver mounts effective immune responses against arriving tumor cells is not fully understood. Using intravital imaging, we have visualized the initial steps of liver metastasis and delineated three phases in the immune response at the earliest stages of liver metastasis: first, there is continuous surveillance of the liver parenchyma by discrete immune cell subsets in the premetastatic tissue. Second, upon metastatic cell arrival, there is massive neutrophil recruitment and tumor-cell material uptake mediated by resident macrophages. Third, antitumor-specific T-cell activation takes place in situ within intrahepatic leukocyte clusters. We find that tumor-derived material uptake triggers transcriptional programs in liver myeloid cells that upregulate chemoattraction programs in Kupffer cells and cDCs, leading to T-cell activation. Antigen cross-presentation and a functional partnership between cDC1s and local macrophages to recruit and form T-cell activation clusters are required for the elicitation of these intrahepatic T-cell responses. Consequently, prior expansion of cDCs by Flt3L-Ig treatment significantly enhances immunosurveillance, curtailing successful metastasis development. Collectively, our findings identify coordinated immune responses that are essential for anti-metastatic immunity within the liver, uncovering a program to mount defenses against tumor cells arriving in the liver.

items.title: Age- and sex-related variation in TREC and KREC and the association of rs2204985 with TREC in adults
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Chemical Biology and Fundamental Medicine
items.abstract: Background: T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC) and kappa-deleting recombination excision circles (KREC) are indirect markers of new T- and B-cell production. Recorded zero values complicate the analysis of age-related and genetic associations in adult cohorts. Methods: We analyzed 574 adult outpatients aged 39-95 years, including 250 men and 324 women. TREC and KREC were quantified by multiplex real-time PCR and normalized per 100,000 cells. The rs2204985 variant was evaluated using age- and sex-adjusted genetic models. A two-part model separated TREC positivity from quantitative TREC levels among participants with positive values. Alternative regressions and receiver operating characteristic analyses were used for sensitivity and age-classification analyses. Results: Age was more strongly associated with log10(TREC + 0.1) than with log10(KREC + 0.1) (beta = -0.0365 and -0.00728 per year, respectively). Women had higher levels in the main-effects models, although the KREC age association differed by sex. There was no clear evidence of an additive rs2204985 association with TREC positivity (odds ratio = 0.836, p = 0.290). Among the 481 TREC-positive participants, the G allele was associated with higher log10(TREC) (beta = +0.0688 per allele, 95% CI +0.0177 to +0.1199, p = 0.0084; q = 0.0126 across three conditional genetic-model tests). Smearing-corrected marginal predictions for a 58-year-old woman were 40.4 copies/100,000 cells for AA and 53.5 for GG. In the common-positive subset (n = 465), TREC showed higher age-classification AUCs than KREC or their ratio. Conclusions: The rs2204985 association was apparent in conditional TREC levels but not in recorded positivity or full-cohort regression. Analyzing these outcomes separately makes the association easier to interpret, without establishing that zero TREC denotes absent thymopoiesis or that the variant directly alters thymic function.

items.title: Agreement between structure prediction tools does not indicate biological plausibility in cancer fusion proteins
items.abstract: While protein-folding software has made great strides in recent years, reliability is known to be poorer on novel structures and failure modes are not fully characterised. Cancer fusion proteins present a unique case of proteins absent from model training data but constructed from parents with known structures. This study tests four popular protein-folding tools on three categories of protein: control, cancer-associated, and uncharacterised fusion proteins. We assessed computational performance, accuracy, and distinct failure modes. For well-characterised proteins, all tools tested returned the correct structures in all but one case, with some tools returning an average of two distinct structural forms in the exception. For characterised cancer-associated proteins, most predictions were highly accurate; poorer predictions often still returned some consistent high-confidence domains but produced divergent results in other areas that were both variable between tools and at odds with experimental structures. For cancer fusion proteins having available parent-protein reference structures, results fell into two clear categories. Roughly half contained structures matching to the functional domains of their parent proteins at high confidence, in keeping with biological expectation for these proteins; the others contained little evidence of matching structures, independent of the tool used. Predictions for fusion proteins differed far more between tools than those for characterised proteins with a median inter-tool TM-score 0.272 versus 0.853 respectively. However, agreement between tools did not indicate a more biologically plausible prediction. For example, all tools predicted drastically different structures for fusion protein TMPRSS2-ERG, but all predictions still contained the core ERG functional domains; conversely, all tools produced highly consistent structures for DNAJB1-PRKACA, but none of the predictions contained the expected functional regions. We recommend that users of these tools use care and caution in the assessments of outputs and consider biological knowledge before blindly trusting results.

items.title: Joint Estimation of Mother and Daughter Protein Regulatory Networks Quantifies Inheritance in Yeast Lineages
items.abstract: Live-cell imaging tracks multiple protein levels within individual cells across divisions in real time, enabling direct measurement of how regulatory dynamics are inherited by a daughter cell from her mother. This technology presents a unique opportunity to directly observe longitudinal dynamics, in contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing, which can only measure cells cross-sectionally. However, there is a lack of computational methods for analyzing live-cell imaging data. Existing frameworks based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) estimate networks from individual time series, but adapting them to mother-daughter pairs poses a dilemma: pooling both cells forces complete inheritance, while fitting each cell separately starves the short daughter trajectory of timepoints needed for reliable estimation. To address this gap, we develop PRNODE (Protein Regulatory Networks via ODEs), which models each cell's network as a deviation from a shared regulatory scaffold and estimates the scaffold and both deviations jointly under a fused group-lasso penalty. The mother's longer time series thereby supports the daughter's estimate, while allowing the two networks to differ wherever the data demand it. We then propose a novel measure of inheritance based on comparing the rate of change of protein levels between the mother's and daughter's networks. Across simulation studies, we find that PRNODE outperforms existing ODE estimation methods in recovering the networks of daughter cells and in estimating inheritance. Finally, we apply PRNODE to many mother-daughter pairs of Saccharomyces cerevisiae observed over a 9-hour period at 12-minute intervals. Many estimated networks show a negative feedback loop between the cell-cycle inhibitor Whi5 and the cyclin Clb2, which together sustain cell-cycle oscillations. We also find that the measured inheritance tracks the number of regulatory edges a daughter shares with her mother with the same sign, more than the presence of any single edge. PRNODE is available as an R package at https://github.com/shirmath/LIC_methods.

items.title: Multiscale superinformation reveals structured organization of genomic sequence features
items.abstract: Genomic sequence organization varies across spatial scales, but sequence complexity measures are often evaluated at a single resolution. Superinformation (SI), introduced by Bose and Chouhan, measures heterogeneity in local sequence entropy by taking the entropy of the distribution of block-level Shannon entropy values. We characterize SI across 14 Sequence Ontology-defined genomic feature classes in seven species and seven block sizes from 20 to 200 bp. SI profiles were non-increasing for 72 of 86 evaluable species-feature combinations, although this pattern was not universal. Observed SI generally exceeded both a block-count-controlled random null and a species-level GC-controlled null. Associations with mononucleotide entropy, dinucleotide entropy, and GC content were modest, with no individual descriptor explaining more than 10.4% of the observed variation. For the 13 complete feature-level profiles used in geometric analysis, the first two principal components explained 97.859% of the variance, and hierarchical clustering grouped features with similar SI trajectories. We also summarize the profiles using the Characteristic Information Scale and Information Persistence Score. These analyses extend the original superinformation framework to a comparative, multiscale analysis of genomic feature heterogeneity while keeping the interpretation of SI limited to the sequence properties measured here.

items.title: deeprok: highly accurate prokaryotic gene prediction through deep learning and overlap-aware decoding
items.corresponding_institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard University
items.abstract: Prokaryotic gene prediction is often considered solved, yet widely used tools still disagree on many genes, chiefly short genes and translation starts. We present deeprok, an ab initio prokaryotic gene prediction method that combines a base-level neural network with an overlap-aware decoder, and refines start-site predictions with a self-trained neural ranker. On four curated genomes distant from its training data, deeprok made 10-18% fewer exact-match errors than Prodigal and GeneMarkS-2, and on 2,925 experimentally verified starts it made 21-41% fewer start errors. Furthermore, deeprok's base-level architecture reveals lineage-specific translation initiation signals. These results show that per-base deep learning combined with overlap-aware decoding can improve prokaryotic gene prediction, especially for resolving translation starts.

items.title: TrailMix: Mixture Proportion and Placement Estimation of Ancient Hominin mtDNA Samples using a Pangenomic Reference
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Health Technology, Section for Bioinformatics, Technical University of Denmark, Kongens Lyngby, Denmark, Department of Computer Science and Softwa
items.abstract: Hominin mitochondrial DNA extracted from sediments or ancient environments is sometimes a mixture of multiple contributing sources. Researchers must subsequently computationally identify from which mitochondrial lineages the DNA sequences comes (e.g. Denisovan vs. modern human superhaplogroup) and ideally, quantify their abundance. Bioinformatics approaches described in the literature to achieve this involve in-house scripts or heuristics applied to tools designed for other datasets. However, such approaches have neither been fully tested nor do they provide credible intervals on model parameters. To address this, we introduce TrailMix, a C++ program for estimating contributing mixture proportions as well as individual source placements on the hominin mitochondrial tree for ancient environmental DNA. Using a pangenome reference graph to mitigate reference-related bias, TrailMix works well to accurately deconvolve mixtures of multiple mitochondrial lineages and place each contributor within its respective phylogenetic context. Crucially, it allows users to place minor contributing sources on the tree even on ancestral nodes without needing to reach consensus in the presence of multiple sources. TrailMix is part of the vgan suite of tools and is available at https://github.com/grenaud/vgan.

items.title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
items.abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

items.title: Zero-shot virtual knock-out rankings do not recover causal genes from observational single-cell data
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Shanxi Provincial People's Hospital Affiliated to Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, 030012, Shanxi, China
items.abstract: Background: Virtual knock-out methods rank genes by the change predicted after deleting one gene in silico and nominate targets without perturbation data. That use assumes the ranking reflects the causal consequence of removal; we tested it for three zero-shot methods in four configurations under one criterion. Results: We compared scTenifoldKnk (R and Python), CellOracle and Geneformer on 438 real, 3,585 synthetic and 330 DepMap knock-outs. Top-20 lists of different knock-outs overlapped by a median of 12 to 14 of 20, against 0.08 by chance. Displacement followed out-degree (R^2 = 0.825; 0.852 with six further features). Decoupling causal effect from topology left criterion value and grade unchanged (36 of 36 RED). For scTenifoldKnk, the ranking showed no evidence of recovery above chance where causal genes were planted (AUROC 0.538 and 0.528 in the two constructions). CellOracle's displacement showed no detectable relation to the data-built network (rho = -0.212, P = 0.556). Geneformer's shift tracked token coverage inconsistently (+0.41, +0.40, -0.27). Against DepMap essentiality, scTenifoldKnk's Python implementation (scTenifoldpy 0.5.1) reached AUROC 0.459 (95% CI 0.357-0.566), not distinguishable from chance; detection rate reached 0.588 (95% CI 0.497-0.677). Conclusions: For scTenifoldKnk and CellOracle, the ranking reports network properties, not the causal consequence of removal. No measured structural feature accounted for more than a small fraction of Geneformer's shift. Detection rate, needing no network, gained +0.129 (95% CI 0.0017-0.2543; 97.6% of resamples positive) over the tool.

items.title: Adjuvant myeloperoxidase inhibition promotes B and T cell mediated control of murine melanoma metastasis
items.abstract: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from primary tumors to distant organs and accounts for the majority of melanoma deaths, with a 5-year survival rate of only 30%. Despite strong evidence that myeloid cells promote metastasis, there are limited clinically effective myeloid-directed therapies. Here, we demonstrate that targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO), a myeloid-lineage restricted enzyme, significantly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden using an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma. Adjuvant MPO inhibition remodeled the metastatic microenvironment by a reduction in Ly6G+Ly6C+ myeloid cells and enrichment of B and T cell populations. Importantly, adjuvant MPO inhibitor-mediated metastatic control was dependent upon B, CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells, and rapidly reduced circulating and disseminated tumor cells. MPO inhibition markedly decreased NET release, while NET deficiency and inhibition recapitulated the anti-metastatic effects of targeting MPO, implicating NETs as a potential downstream mediator of MPO-driven metastasis. We further validated these findings in a distinct spontaneous breast cancer model where adjuvant MPO inhibition similarly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden with comparable changes within the metastatic immune microenvironment. Collectively, our studies introduce MPO as a druggable regulator of metastasis where MPO inhibition limits metastatic disease by targeting immunosuppressive myeloid cells.

items.title: Cognitive Load modulates the exploration-exploitation trade-off Through Reconfiguration of an IPS-Centered Decision Network
items.corresponding_institution: Southern Medical University School of Public Health
items.abstract: In dynamic environments where rewards continuously change, adaptive decision-making requires ongoing updates of option-value and uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. This process depends on cognitive resources and involves coordinated interactions among multiple brain regions; however, how cognitive load affects directed exploration in such dynamic environments, and whether these effects are accompanied by changes in interactions among exploration-related brain regions, remains unclear. We embedded a working-memory load manipulation within a dynamic four-armed bandit task. Experiment 1 compared computational models and quantified load-related changes in exploration; Experiment 2 examined these behavioral effects in an independent sample and investigated their neural correlates using fMRI. Across both experiments, high load reduced the uncertainty bonus parameter ({varphi}), indicating weaker directed exploration. Experiment 2 additionally showed lower inverse temperature ({beta}) under high load, indicating more stochastic choices. Directed exploration relative to exploitation more activated the frontopolar cortex (FP), intraparietal sulcus (IPS), anterior insula (aIns), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses indicated stronger functional coupling between the right aIns and IPS under low load. Guided by the candidate connections identified by PPI, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) focused on a three-region subnetwork. Bayesian model selection favored the model with directed-exploration-related input to the IPS, while condition-specific comparisons suggested stronger aIns-to-IPS effective connectivity under low load. Together, these findings link cognitive resource demands to reduced uncertainty-guided directed exploration in a dynamic environment and suggest that this behavioral change is accompanied by selective reconfiguration of interactions within an IPS-centered decision subnetwork.

items.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
items.abstract: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

items.title: Transmural compression drives lymphatic endothelial dysfunction through Piezo1-CaMKII signaling
items.corresponding_institution: Institut des Maladies Metaboliques et Cardiovasculaires
items.abstract: Background: Secondary lymphedema is characterized by progressive lymphatic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and tissue fibrosis, but how mechanical changes during disease progression contribute to lymphatic failure remains poorly understood. Lymphatic vessels initially undergo intraluminal pressure-induced dilation, whereas advanced disease is associated with extraluminal compression resulting from tissue remodeling. We investigated how these different mechanical stimuli affect lymphatic endothelial function. Methods and Results: We developed a human lymphatic vessel-on-chip model enabling independent control of intra- and extraluminal pressure. In contrast to vessel dilation, extraluminal compression profoundly disrupted lymphatic endothelial barrier integrity, increasing permeability and causing junctional disorganization, while also inducing a strong pro-inflammatory transcriptional response. Mechanistically, compression induced sustained intracellular Ca2 influx and activated the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1. Piezo1 inhibition attenuated compression-induced Ca2 responses and protected endothelial barrier integrity, identifying Piezo1 as an upstream mediator of compression-induced dysfunction. Downstream, compression-induced Ca2 signaling activated Ca2 /calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), whose inhibition preserved endothelial junctional integrity and reduced both barrier dysfunction and inflammatory activation. In a murine model of secondary lymphedema, CaMKII inhibition improved lymphatic function and reduced lymphedema-associated tissue remodeling. Conclusions: These findings identify a Piezo1-CaMKII signaling axis that links pathological extraluminal compression to lymphatic endothelial dysfunction and inflammation. Targeting this pathway may help preserve lymphatic function during lymphedema progression.

items.title: A specialized extracellular matrix patterns the conserved cortical protein EFA-6 at neuron-epidermal interfaces
items.abstract: Sensory neurons establish intimate connections with the surrounding epidermis, where specialized extracellular matrix (ECM) help maintain neuron-epidermal interactions. However, whether and how this specialized ECM regulates the spatial organization of cortical proteins at these interfaces remains poorly understood. Here, we show a specialized ECM patterns the cortical microtubule regulator EFA-6 at neuron-epidermal interfaces in Caenorhabditis elegans. We show that EFA-6 in the epidermal cortex is enriched adjacent to the neurites of touch receptor neurons, characterized by discrete foci at the distal neurite and a diffuse distribution in the proximal neurite. We identify the specialized ECM components MEC-1 and HIM-4/hemicentin as regulators of EFA-6 spatial patterning at the interface between epidermis and neuronal processes. EFA-6 proteins contain an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) that is necessary and sufficient for EFA-6 targeting to and patterning at the neuron-epidermal interface. Within the IDR, we further identify an 8 residue motif that regulates enrichment and patterning of EFA-6 IDR at this interface. Finally, we find that EFA-6 contributes to age-dependent neurite defects in him-4 mutants. Together, our findings reveal how a specialized extracellular matrix and an intrinsically disordered region coordinate the spatial organization of a cortical MT regulator at neuron-epidermal interface.

items.title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
items.corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
items.abstract: Quantitative comparison of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag datasets is complicated when a perturbation changes the global abundance of the profiled chromatin feature or when there is substantial variability between replicates. Read-depth normalization removes global differences by design, whereas exogenous spike-in normalization can introduce substantial technical variability. We developed Background-Anchored SIgnal Normalization (BASIN), an endogenous-reference framework that exploits recurrent, peak-like background in IgG controls as a quantitative internal reference. BASIN Anchor Regions (BARs) act as reproducible read sinks whose representation rises as specific signal falls, allowing global differences to be inferred from the balance between specific and nonspecific reads. BASIN comprises three pipelines: OVERTURE identifies and evaluates BAR panels, HARMONY derives and applies robust sample-specific scale factors from trimmed BAR signal, and CODA determines whether the assumptions supporting normalization are satisfied. BASIN provides a validated, ready-to-use universal BAR panel for Drosophila melanogaster, and the OVERTURE pipeline enables BAR panel development in other organisms. We tested BASIN against independent expectations and compared its performance with spike-in normalization. BASIN remained quantitatively stable across a >100-fold cell-input titration and detected global depletion of H3K36me3 in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. BASIN also preserved expected H3K9me3 differences even when target signal overlapped anchor regions. Applied to a variety of profiling experiments, CODA distinguished normalization failures arising from both biological and technical causes. BASIN thus converts reproducible background from a nuisance signal into an internal reference standard, enabling spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes while providing an explicit framework to test when and why that normalization can or cannot be trusted.

items.title: Effects of sequence splitting and negative-set selection on antimicrobial peptide prediction
items.abstract: Sequence partitioning and negative-set selection determine the prediction problem posed by an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) benchmark. We quantified their effects using a DRAMP 5.0 audit, controlled comparisons with frozen ESM-2 classifiers and additional benchmark configurations. On DRAMP, random splitting increased Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.718 under cluster-disjoint splitting to 0.932. This difference of 0.214 exceeded the gains from the architectural additions tested, and 75.6% of randomly assigned test sequences shared a homology cluster with training sequences. Across three additional dataset configurations, random-minus-cluster MCC differences ranged from -0.04634 to +0.05682, showing that the magnitude and direction of the split effect depended on benchmark composition. With the fitted classifiers and APD6 positives held fixed, replacing DRAMP test negatives with external hard negatives reduced the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.9833 to 0.9018 (paired difference 0.08149, bootstrap 95% CI 0.07196 to 0.09181). These comparisons quantify substantial sensitivity to evaluation design and show why split effects require assessment within each benchmark. AMPBenchAudit provides the audited records, split assignments and evaluation code needed to examine this sensitivity and interpret model comparisons under explicit test conditions.

items.title: Compensatory Creatine Secretion Protects Against Drug-Induced Liver Injury via Desuccinylation
items.corresponding_institution: Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital, Guangdong Academy of Medical Sciences, Southern Medical University
items.abstract: ackground and aims: Effective therapeutic interventions for Drug induced liver injury (DILI) remain limited. N-myc downstream regulated gene-1 (NDRG1), a stress-responsive proteins, has an incompletely defined role in acetaminophen-induced liver injury. Method: Wild-type (WT), NDRG1Hep-flox, Hepatocyte-specific NDRG1 conditional knockout mice (NDRG1Hep-KO) were subjected to APAP-induced injury modeling. Liver and blood sample from patient were analyzed. Liver sample of mice subsequently underwent RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), untargeted metabolomic profiling, single-cell sequencing, succinylation sequencing. For in vitro studies, AML-12 hepatocytes, RAW264.7 macrophages, and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs), human Monocyte-Derived Macrophages, human hepatocyte organoids were utilized in experiments. Result: NDRG1 was upregulated in mouse and human DILI livers. NDRG1 conditional knockout significantly exacerbates DILI. Mechanistically, NDRG1 inhibited GAMT ubiquitination to enhance creatine production, and hepatocyte?derived creatine attenuated M1 polarization of liver macrophages by suppressing PHB1 succinylation at lysine 128. CXCL2? macrophages were identified as a major subpopulation regulated by NDRG1. Conclusion: Hepatocyte NDRG1 protects against APAP-DILI by driving GAMT-dependent creatine production and PHB1 K128 succinylation-dependent macrophage reprogramming.

items.title: APOBEC3 Activation Drives Epitranscriptomic Remodeling and Clonal Hematopoiesis
items.abstract: Stress and inflammatory cytokine-inducible APOBEC3 (A3) enzymes promote clonal evolution in many malignancies. We identified A3C overexpression in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) following spaceflight-associated accelerated aging and in precancer myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). However, the role of A3 in age-associated clonal hematopoiesis (CH) and precancer initiation remains unclear. To investigate the functional hierarchy among A3 enzymes, we performed lentiviral A3B, A3C, A3D, A3F, and A3G overexpression, whole genome, whole transcriptome and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses, and functional HSPC assays. While A3C and A3F induced more C-to-T DNA mutations; A3B, A3C, and A3G deregulated RNA splicing; and all A3 enzymes induced C-to-U RNA edits in HSPCs. In aged HSPCs, A3C overexpression enhanced replating and myeloid lineage skewing in humanized inflammatory niche mouse models typical of CH. Moreover, A3C-induced editing of CH-associated transcripts distinguished MPN from normal HSPCs. Thus, future strategies focused on APOBEC3C inhibition may prevent CH and precancer initiation.

items.title: Monolayer, Spheroid, and Organoid Formats Elicit Proteomic States that Couple Organelle Organization to Metabolic Vulnerabilities
items.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) cell culture systems are becoming more widely applied to model tissue organization, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Yet, the molecular characteristics that distinguish organoids and spheroids from conventional monolayer culture are incompletely defined. Here, using tumorigenic organoid models of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian cancer (HGSC), we establish a quantitative proteomic resource that reveals how cell architecture and media independently but jointly shape the cellular state in organoids, spheroids, and monolayers. We further pursue HGSC subtype-enriched features within this framework and identify that a poor prognosis-associated genotype with reported paclitaxel hypersensitivity, Trp53-/-;Pten-/-;Nf1-/- (PPN), is marked by increased microtubule-associated proteins, lipid-associated factors, and mitochondrial remodeling. PPN cells displayed clustered lipid droplets, whereby mitochondria-ER tethering increased. Relative to Trp53-/- (P) and a frequent HGSC genotype, Trp53-/-;Brca1+/-;MycOE (PBM), live-cell imaging showed that PPN exhibits the highest degree of stable mitochondria-ER encapsulations, coincident with fission-biased mitochondria and a high-flux respiratory state. Disruption of the mitochondria-ER contact protein PTPIP51 reduced lipid droplet clustering in the PPN state. Because cytomegalovirus is known to exploit host mitochondria remodeling, mitochondria-ER contacts, and metabolic output during infection, we tested whether this pre-existing host configuration is associated with cytomegalovirus permissiveness. PPN organoids exhibited greater murine cytomegalovirus infection and infectious output than matched monolayers or PBM. Together, these data define a resource of distinct protein characteristics between matched monolayer, spheroid, and organoid systems that should be considered for experimental design. We also uncover a mechanistic axis connecting 3D architecture, organelle contacts, metabolism, drug response, and viral permissiveness.

items.title: Evaluation of a Brief Educational Intervention to Improve Healthcare Provider Communication About Autism Genetic Testing
items.abstract: Although professional guidelines recommend offering genetic testing following an autism diagnosis, uptake remains low in the United States. Healthcare providers frequently report limited education and uncertainty discussing autism genetics with patients and families. We developed and evaluated a brief educational intervention to improve provider communication about autism genetic testing, consisting of animated videos addressing autism genetics, available testing options, and strategies for discussing testing with autistic individuals and families. We evaluated the intervention among 100 U.S.-based healthcare providers and a community panel of 99 autistic adults. Participants completed a validated measure of genetic literacy before viewing the videos, then evaluated the intervention and its perceived impact on genetic testing. Providers showed higher genetic literacy than the general U.S. population, yet only 23% reported frequently discussing genetic testing before the intervention. Afterward, 86% reported greater likelihood of recommending genetic testing following diagnosis, and 88% reported the videos changed how they would discuss genetics with patients and families. Both cohorts rated the resources favorably, and 71% of autistic adults reported greater likelihood of pursuing genetic testing after viewing the videos. Brief, communication-focused educational resources may improve workflows for autism genetic testing and support informed decision-making for providers, autistic individuals, and their families.

items.title: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
items.abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

items.title: Escape from X-chromosome inactivation increases disease risk and drives sex-differential genetic effects: a population-scale PheXWAS
items.abstract: X chromosome (Xchr) contribution to complex traits remains incomplete, due to its unique inheritance pattern and its inactivation mechanism. Therefore, we gathered data from 800,000 individuals from the UK Biobank and dbGaP, and performed a sex-stratified phenome-wide association study of Xchr variation across 3,741 complex traits. Heritability analyses revealed sex-specific patterns and an overall involvement of Xchr in complex phenotypes. We identified 6,531 loci significantly associated with 402 complex traits, with a higher proportion of associations consistent with dominant inheritance than observed for autosomes. Although effect directions were largely concordant between sexes, loci with significant effect-size differences were enriched for escape-gene associations. Escape genes were depleted among trait-associated loci and strongly enriched for risky disease effects. These association patterns enabled prediction of escape status for unannotated genes. This overview of Xchr contribution to complex traits suggests inactivation escape as a clear risky feature for females.

items.title: Transcriptional aging across CNS tissues in the ALS-FTD spectrum reflects clock architecture and disease-associated cellular signatures
items.abstract: Background. We examined transcriptomic (gene expression-based) aging in postmortem central nervous system (CNS) tissues from donors across the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-frontotemporal dementia (FTD) spectrum and investigated the molecular and cellular features underlying disease-associated differences in transcriptional aging clocks. Methods. Six transcriptomic clocks (RNAAgeCalc DESeq2, GTExAge, Pearson and GenAge; Pasta REG and age-shift) were applied to 2,235 RNA-sequencing samples from 609 donors across 11 CNS regions, with adjustment for age and tissue-specific technical variables. We compared transcriptional age across ALS, ALS-FTD, FTD, and controls, examining regional variation, gene-level contributions, cell composition, disease duration, and C9orf72 status, with independent validation of gene contributions in a cervical spinal cord cohort. Results. Disease-associated differences in transcriptional age varied by diagnosis, tissue, and clock. ALS and ALS-FTD showed the strongest differences in spinal cord, while FTD differences localized primarily to the frontal and temporal cortex. In ALS spinal cord, RNAAgeCalc DESeq2 estimates were lower than controls, whereas other clocks estimated higher transcriptional age when significant. CHIT1 was identified as the primary contributor to the DESeq2 transcriptional age decrease in ALS. Cell composition adjustment attenuated ALS spinal cord differences, reflecting microglial, lymphocyte, oligodendrocyte, and astrocyte signatures, though the lumbar GenAge increase in transcriptional age and DESeq2 decrease remained significant. The higher transcriptional age in ALS motor cortex also remained significantafter adjustment. Clinical associations were likewise clock dependent. Higher spinal DESeq2 age acceleration (AA) was associated with longer ALS duration, though this association was strongly influenced by the CHIT1 term. Higher GTExAge AA in cervical spinal cord, thoracic spinal cord, and occipital cortex was associated with shorter disease duration; no significant associations were observed for the other clock-tissue combinations or for ALS-FTD. No clock differed by C9orf72 repeat expansion status. Conclusions. In this study we found disease-associated differences in transcriptional age that localize to clinically relevant tissues. Differences in transcriptional aging across the ALS-FTD spectrum reflect interactions among clock architecture, disease-associated gene expression, tissue region, and cellular composition. Resolving these components reveals the biological context underlying divergent clock estimates and provides a framework for interpreting changes in transcriptional aging.

items.title: Smartphone-Based Assessment of Cognitive Variability in Alzheimer Disease
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Repeated smartphone testing can measure cognitive inconsistency that a single clinic visit cannot capture. We evaluated cognitive variability and everyday phone use in biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer disease (AD). METHODS: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment due to AD or mild AD dementia and cognitively unimpaired controls used Smartphone Monitoring Assessment in Real Time-Alzheimer (SMART-A) on their own phones. Response-time variability was adjusted for task demand and practice. RESULTS: Among 26 participants with cognitive data (14 controls, 12 AD), the four-marker variability composite was higher in AD (Hedges g = 1.29; 95% confidence interval, 0.53-2.06; P = .003) and correlated with baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment score (r = -0.60; P = .001). Memory-task accuracy was lower in AD at all four trials, and 64.5% versus 98.2% of sessions reached delayed recall (P < .001). Median phone-use bouts were shorter in AD (2.4 vs 5.4 minutes; P = .031), without a detectable pickup-frequency difference. Diary-reported bedtime was earlier in AD; sensor-derived sleep, activity, and mobility showed no statistically detectable differences. None of the 19 cross-domain contrasts survived false-discovery-rate correction. DISCUSSION: SMART-A supported repeated assessment over months in biomarker-confirmed AD. Cognitive variability, memory-task progression, and phone-use duration are promising complementary measures, requiring independent validation of reliability, incremental value, and sensitivity to clinical change.

items.title: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
items.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

items.title: The Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (C-PIP) Reference Sample: Study Design, Recruitment Strategy, and Phenotyping Protocol
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry and Addiction, Faculty of Medicine, Universite de Montreal; Azrieli Research Center, CHU Sainte Justine Mother Child University Hospita
items.abstract: Distinguishing atypical from typical neurodevelopment requires large, well-characterized paediatric cohorts with harmonized multimodal neuroimaging and comprehensive phenotyping. Here, we describe the protocol for the Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (CPIP) Reference Sample, including the design, recruitment strategy, and phenotyping protocol, along with overviews of the imaging and genetics protocols. Using a multisite accelerated longitudinal design, we aim to recruit >800 participants aged 0 to 16 years at baseline, across three Canadian sites (Alberta Childrens Hospital, Calgary; The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Toronto; and CHU Sainte-Justine, Montreal) with comprehensive assessments at baseline and an annual follow-up, with additional follow-ups contingent on project extension. The protocol includes harmonized multimodal neuroimaging, extensive phenotyping across five broad domains: demographic, social and environmental factors; physical health and development; mental health and substance use; cognition; and temperament/personality, as well as DNA sequencing. Exclusion criteria are minimal to ensure a sample representative of the catchment areas of the participating hospitals. Data and protocols will be openly shared with the research community. The C-PIP Reference Sample will provide Canada's first large-scale pediatric neuroimaging reference cohort, enabling researchers to map typical and atypical trajectories from infancy through adolescence, identify biomarkers, examine genetic and contextual influences on brain development, and provide a normative comparison framework for clinical populations.

items.title: Panel-agnostic tumour-only diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency
items.abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.

items.title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors
items.abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

items.title: CB-COMIL: interpretable prediction of melanoma immunotherapyresponse from multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images
items.abstract: Deep learning models can predict melanoma immunotherapy response but rarely explain predictions biologically. Concept bottleneck models offer interpretable predictions, but have not been applied to multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and whether their learned concepts reproduce tissue measurements remains unclear. We developed CB-COMIL, which routes mIF predictions through four supervised concepts (immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index), decomposing each prediction exactly into concept contributions. Developed on 211 slides and evaluated on 42 slides from an independent, differently acquired test cohort, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020, 95% CI: -0.103 to 0.144). In 41 slides with complete measurements, learned concepts correlated with measured counterparts (Spearman: 0.61; 0.61-0.76), yet substituting measured values reduced macro-F1 from 0.68 to 0.48. CB-COMIL makes predictions interpretable without detectable performance loss, and our evaluation shows that concepts can faithfully determine predictions without reproducing the corresponding biological measurements.

items.title: Exome sequencing in individuals with oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome provides further evidence of a non-traditional inheritance model
items.abstract: The oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome is a rare condition characterized by ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, mandibular hypoplasia, preauricular tags, and ear anomalies. Despite presenting a clinically recognizable pattern defined by the overlap of craniofacial microsomia and frontonasal dysplasia, its etiology remains unknown. Males and females are equally affected, and there is no recurrence reported. Genetic investigations performed to date could not clarify this issue yet. To further investigate Mendelian inheritance and test the hypothesis of a possible monogenic cause, we performed exome sequencing in a case series of Brazilian individuals from a single center with the clinical diagnosis of oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome, including both solo and trio-based exome sequencing. The results provided here further support a non-traditional inheritance model, requiring additional studies including multi-omics approaches to elucidate its etiology.

items.title: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
items.abstract: Background: The majority of rare diseases are caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene with Mendelian inheritance. In contrast, common diseases typically have complex genetic etiology, ranging from a cumulative impact of many common genetic variants with small individual effects, to fewer rare variants with larger effects, with monogenic forms at the rare end of the spectrum. While unknown prevalence of the monogenic fraction of common diseases and incomplete penetrance make identification of such monogenic forms of common diseases particularly challenging, their diagnosis can be essential for precision medicine. Automated rare variant prioritization tools, such as Exomiser, aid whole exome sequencing-based rare genetic disease diagnostics. However, Exomiser's utility has not been systematically assessed in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases prior to this study. Methods: We evaluated and optimized Exomiser for prioritization of rare pathogenic variants in common disease using a large kidney stone disease (KSD) cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). First, we benchmarked Exomiser's performance across different settings for KSD "gold standard" variants in established KSD genes with Mendelian inheritance. Next, we utilized the optimal pipeline for discovery of novel KSD genes and compared Exomiser's findings with results from gene-level rare variant enrichment analyses in an extended in-house cohort and the UK Biobank. Results: With the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all (94%, N = 48) previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated 62 novel genes predominantly involved in ion homeostasis, which are now available to the scientific community as candidate genes for KSD. Out of these genes, orthogonal approaches also support ABCC6 as a strong KSD risk gene, in line with previous research, providing a proof-of-principle supporting the utility of Exomiser in the context of common disease. Conclusions: This study serves as an example for automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases, which is a key step for precision medicine.

items.title: Remote auditory task performance, cognition, and APOE4 across two dementia-risk cohorts
items.abstract: Background. Difficulty hearing speech in noise is associated with cognitive ageing and dementia risk. It is unclear whether performance on remote auditory tasks reflects the apolipoprotein E (APOE) {epsilon}4 allele, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimers disease, or broader cognitive and ageing processes. Methods. We analysed two independent cohorts: the Great Minds research register of older adults and the mid-life PREVENT Dementia programme. Both completed the same remote auditory battery: digits-in-noise, speech-in-babble, auditory working-memory precision for tone frequency and for amplitude-modulation rate, and the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index. Cognitive outcomes were paired-associate learning in Great Minds, and the Four Mountains Task, Supermarket Task and selected COGNITO scores in PREVENT. Associations were tested with covariate-adjusted robust regression and false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction. Results. The analytic samples comprised 164 Great Minds and 90 PREVENT participants (mean age 70.6 vs 56.8 years). APOE {epsilon}4 carrier status was not associated with any auditory measure in either cohort (all FDR-corrected p>0.70). In Great Minds, better speech-in-babble performance and better amplitude-modulation-rate working-memory precision were each associated with better paired-associate learning (both FDR-corrected p=0.019). In PREVENT, no auditory measure was associated with spatial-memory or COGNITO scores after age and sex adjustment and FDR correction. Conclusions. Remote auditory task performance was associated with memory in the older cohort but not with APOE {epsilon}4 carrier status in either cohort, although the samples could not exclude small genotype effects. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether remote auditory testing predicts cognitive change.

items.title: Interrater agreement of seizure onset and spread in scalp EEG
items.abstract: Objective. Faster seizure spread on intracranial EEG has been linked to worse surgical outcome. If contralateral spread on scalp EEG carried similar prognostic information, it could identify poor resection candidates before intracranial monitoring and direct them toward neuromodulation sooner. Testing this first requires that experts reliably annotate spread on scalp EEG. The interrater agreement for seizure spread detection on scalp EEG is unknown; prior scalp EEG reliability studies have focused mainly on seizure detection. We quantified expert agreement on the laterality, channels, and timing of seizure onset and contralateral spread. Methods. We retrospectively analyzed 79 seizures from 48 patients undergoing presurgical evaluation at a single center. Three board certified epileptologists independently marked the time and channels of onset and contralateral spread for each seizure. We measured agreement on onset laterality and spread presence with Gwet k, channels with Cohen k, and timing with the median absolute deviation (MAD). Interrater and majority vote consensus agreement were estimated with patient-clustered CIs. Results. Onset laterality showed substantial interrater agreement (Gwet k = 0.73, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.83); most disagreement involved bilateral onsets. Contralateral spread agreement was comparable (0.63, 0.48 to 0.76). Channel level agreement was higher for onset (inter rater Cohen k = 0.57) than for spread (0.38). Onset timing was highly consistent (median MAD 0.40 s); spread timing agreement was also high (1.99 s), but less so than onset timing (sign rank p < 0.001). Agreement did not differ across annotators or between temporal and non-temporal epilepsy. Significance. Epileptologists generally agree on onset laterality and whether and when seizures spread contralaterally, although spread channels are identified less reliably. These findings support the feasibility of measuring scalp EEG spread as a candidate noninvasive marker of seizure network extent. The public annotated dataset provides a multi-expert reference standard for developing automated spread detection algorithms.

items.title: Geographic heterogeneity of gut microbiome biomarkers across neurological conditions: sub-national discordance in ten cohorts from eleven cities in six countries
items.abstract: Gut microbiota composition has been associated with multiple neurological conditions, and candidate biomarkers have been proposed on the basis of these associations. Their usefulness presupposes that taxa altered in one population are also altered in others, a condition that is rarely verified. This work quantifies the extent to which it holds, and the geographic scale at which it ceases to do so. Ten public 16S rRNA gene sequencing cohorts of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and autism spectrum disorder, collected in eleven cities across six countries, were reprocessed from raw data, comprising 1,185 samples with uniform processing within each condition. Models trained and evaluated within a single cohort reached a mean AUC of 0.751 in Alzheimer's disease, 0.741 in autism spectrum disorder and 0.673 in Parkinson's disease. When applied to a different population, these values fell to 0.569, 0.542 and 0.551 respectively. The decline was not associated with geographic distance: transfer between cities within the same country was equivalent to transfer between continents. No taxon appeared among the twenty most important features in all cohorts of a given condition, and no correlation between rankings reached significance. Classifiers trained to predict cohort of origin, disregarding clinical group, reached AUC values of 0.87 to 1.00 using control subjects, and equivalent values using affected subjects. In one cohort with two recruitment centers and a single protocol, controls from both cities were separable (AUC 0.947), models did not transfer between centers (0.562 and 0.515), and their rankings correlated 0.003. Geographic heterogeneity of discriminant taxa operates below the national scale, which constrains the generalization of microbiome signatures derived from individual cohorts.

items.title: Spatially localized racial differences in the association between white matter hyperintensities and verbal memory in cognitively unimpaired adults
items.abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are common in aging, but whether their cognitive associations differ between African American and White older adults is unclear. We studied 5,187 cognitively unimpaired non-Hispanic African American (NHA) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) older adults across three independent cohorts using depth- and lobe-resolved WMH mapping with cross-sectional, longitudinal and machine learning analyses. In the Emory Healthy Brain Study (EHBS), greater WMH burden was more strongly associated with poorer verbal memory among NHA than NHW participants. A similar difference was observed in a 34-center cohort but not detected in the third cohort. Differences localized to frontal juxtacortical and parietal deep white matter in EHBS and the multicenter cohort, respectively, and did not parallel WMH burden distributions. Estimates changed little after adjustment for cohort-specific Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers, vascular risk factors, structural imaging measures and APOE genotype. Accounting for neighborhood deprivation in EHBS yielded a similar estimate. Generalized random forests supported these differences without assuming a linear interaction. Baseline frontal juxtacortical WMH burden showed a stronger association with subsequent AD-signature cortical thinning among NHA than NHW participants in EHBS, with directionally similar multicenter findings. Spatially resolved WMH measures may help identify early heterogeneity in vascular contributions to cognitive aging.

items.title: Spatial proteomics identifies a myeloid-dominated, compartmentalized microenvironment and a proliferation-associated prognostic signature in clear cell sarcoma
items.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is a rare soft-tissue sarcoma with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Because of its rarity, the composition, spatial organization, and functional relevance of the CCS tumour microenvironment and tumour cell heterogeneity remain largely unexplored. Here, to address this gap, and as part of the Clear Cell Sarcoma Consortium, we used imaging mass cytometry with two antibody panels to generate a single-cell, spatially resolved proteomic map of CCS, profiling more than 5 million cells from a multi-institutional, clinically annotated formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded cohort of 52 patients. Our analysis shows that CCS is immune-cold, with the tumour centre dominated by myeloid cells, principally CD68+ and CD163+ macrophages, whereas the invasive front harbours a more diverse, lymphoid-containing immune infiltrate. Within the tumour compartment, we identified a proliferative tumour cell phenotype associated with shorter overall survival. Deep visual proteomics further identified a global proliferation signature enriched for cell-cycle and replication programmes in tumours with high abundance of this phenotype. Further, deep-learning-based models could predict the abundance of the proliferative tumour phenotype in haematoxylin-and-eosin images, which may suggest a path toward future patient stratification in the clinic. Finally, we identified c-MET and B7-H3 as candidate antibody-drug conjugate targets without significant regional or primary-metastasis differences in expression. Together, this work illuminates the spatial proteomic landscape of CCS and highlights candidate markers for patient stratification and potential therapeutic targets.

items.title: Scalable cell-state-resolved TWAS identified dynamic autoimmune disease genes along functional programs
items.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to prioritize genes for complex diseases. TWAS typically trains models on expression quantitative disease locus (eQTL) reference data to predict gene expression from genotype, then tests for association between the predicted expression and disease. With the rapid growth of single-cell eQTL data, there is a pressing need for methods that can fully leverage cell-level information. We previously developed TWiST, the first method for TWAS at cell-state resolution. TWiST is powerful, but training its prediction model is computationally expensive. Here we propose Fast-TWiST, an accelerated and scalable version of TWiST that can analyze hundreds of thousands to millions of cells. Fast-TWiST computes donor-level summary statistics that retain all the information needed to fit the cell-level model, so numerical optimization runs over donors rather than individual cells. In simulations and real-data evaluations, Fast-TWiST was more than 10 times faster than TWiST while matching its statistical performance. Applying the method to the OneK1K data, we identified 3,092 dynamic gene-disease associations that depend on biologically interpretable gene programs, including cytotoxicity, immediate early gene (IEG), BCL2/FAM13A, T helper 1-like (Th1-Like), and resting T helper 2 (Th2-Resting). Independent eQTL datasets and single-cell multiome data supported cell-state-specific regulatory effects that may be driving these findings.

items.title: Genetic analysis of non-familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease patients
items.abstract: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), defined by symptom onset before age 65, can be either familial or sporadic and accounts for approximately 5% of all Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases, with only approximately 10% showing Mendelian inheritance. In this study, we compare the genetic architecture of four cohorts comprising 87 sporadic EOAD cases, 1,018 late-onset AD (LOAD) cases, 585 non-demented controls (TGEN2-AD and TGEN2-ND cohorts), and 3,487 non-demented controls from the AD Sequencing Project (ADSP-CTL). We observed a significant enrichment of the APOE epsilon 4 allele in the EOAD cohort compared to controls (52.2% vs 20.1%; p = 1.54e-10), although its frequency was lower than in the LOAD cohort (64.5%; p = 0.0298). As expected, APOE epsilon 4 was strongly enriched in the LOAD group relative to controls (p = 1.23e-63). Sporadic EOAD genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis and sequence kernel association tests (SKAT) confirmed strong association signals in the APOE locus, including the genes APOE, APOC1, NECTIN2, and TOMM40. AD-related polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis showed that EOAD patients carried an intermediate genetic risk (mean PRS = 40.1), significantly lower than LOAD (mean PRS = 57.5; p = 6.7e-05) but higher than controls (mean PRS = 25.1; p = 6.1e-04). Notably, rare variants in autosomal dominant AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and previously reported EOAD/LOAD modifier genes were not enriched in the sporadic EOAD cohort. These results suggest that, despite earlier onset, sporadic EOAD is not driven by a higher polygenic burden or rare high-impact variants. Instead, its genetic architecture appears to overlap more closely with LOAD, supporting the hypothesis that EOAD may represent an early and more severe manifestation of LOAD or a genetically distinct subtype. Unidentified risk factors, such as epigenetic modifications or complex structural variants, may contribute to EOAD genetic risk and warrant further investigation to better elucidate the complex genetic architecture of Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: Beyond standardized health-related quality of life measures: Additional symptoms and problems reported through the EORTC WISP instrument in the EUonQoL-Kit study across European cancer populations
items.corresponding_institution: Palliative Care Research Unit, Department of Geriatric and Palliative Medicine GP, Copenhagen University Hospital - Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg, University of
items.abstract: Background: Standardized health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures may not capture all symptoms/problems relevant to people with cancer. The European Oncology Quality of Life toolkit (EUonQoL-Kit), co-created with multiple stakeholders to inform health policy across Europe, combines standardized closed-ended patient-reported outcome (PRO) items with the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) open-ended Write In three Symptoms/Problems (WISP) instrument.
