We aimed to identify symptoms/problems reported via WISP beyond the EUonQoL-Kit, examine differences in background characteristics between WISP respondents and non-respondents, and compare additional symptom/problem reporting across three target cancer populations: patients in active treatment, survivors, and patients in palliative care. Methodology: This descriptive analysis used data from adults with current or previous cancer diagnoses participating in a multicenter validation study across 32 European countries (22 August 2024 - 7 July 2025). WISP responses were categorized, and subsequently their prevalence and severity were calculated. Participant characteristics and the ten most frequently reported additional symptoms/problems were compared across groups using t-tests, chi-square tests, or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. Results: Among 4,284 included participants, 519 (12.1%) reported 954 symptoms/problems on WISP, of which 383 (40.1%) were not covered by EUonQoL-Kit v2 closed-ended items. Women, participants from Western and Northern Europe, highly educated and those diagnosed with breast cancer were more likely to respond to the WISP than other subgroups (all p < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were found in the prevalence of common additional symptoms/problems (p [≥] 0.130). Descriptively, numbness/tingling, skin problems and bleeding were most reported by patients in active treatment; indigestion, incontinence, and vision problems in survivors; and edema, cough and itching in palliative care. Conclusions: The EORTC WISP complemented standardized PRO assessment by capturing additional symptoms/problems. Integrating open-ended WISP reporting into the final toolkit may enhance HRQoL assessment across European cancer populations while identifying population-specific concerns without expanding predefined items for all respondents.

items.title: Aneuploidy and structural genome complexity beyond the EWSR1 fusion is associated with evolution and outcome in clear cell sarcoma
authors: Tavares, L. S. P. D. S.
items.corresponding_institution: Research Department of Pathology, UCL Cancer Institute, London, UK
items.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare cancer defined by EWSR1-CREB gene family fusions with clinical outcomes that range from indolent to chemotherapy-refractory metastatic disease. Through multi-omic profiling of primary, recurrent and metastatic tumours and cell lines, we show that CCS is more genomically complex than previously recognised. Beyond the fusion, tumours acquire chromoplexy, chromothripsis and an intermediate aneuploidy burden, with ongoing subclonal diversification. Recurrent events include chromosome17q gain and inactivation of the MYC antagonist MGA. Enriched transcriptional signatures of chromosomal instability,17q gain, 9p21.3 loss and TERT alteration each double the hazard of death, supporting a new molecular based CCS risk stratification framework at diagnosis. Transcriptomes converge on a MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis programme, a previously unrecognised therapeutic vulnerability. These findings address a central paradox of CCS, a shared oncogenic identity with divergent clinical fate, implicating tolerated aneuploidy and chromosomal diversification as candidate determinants of progression.

items.title: Regional brain-age gaps reveal a shared polygenic architecture and regionally patterned clinical and cell-type associations
items.corresponding_institution: Graduate School of Data Science, Seoul National University
items.abstract: A single brain-age estimate may obscure regional differences in clinical vulnerability. Using voxel-level deep learning, we derived whole-brain and nine regional brain-age gaps (BAGs) spanning cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions from T1-weighted MRI in 46,254 UK Biobank participants. Genetic correlation estimates in 41,067 participants (rg = 0.56-0.93) exceeded phenotypic correlations across all 45 pairs, yet regional profiles varied across 24 hospital-recorded diagnoses. Oligodendrocyte annotations predominated for whole-brain and cerebellar BAGs, whereas annotations for caudate BAG included astrocyte and vascular classes. In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, temporal BAG showed stronger associations with cerebrospinal fluid A{beta}42 and cognition than whole-brain BAG when modelled together. A regional model modestly improved discrimination of observed conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease during available follow-up compared with a whole-brain model. Polygenic scores showed cross-cohort associations with hypertension and osteoporosis. Regional BAGs provide complementary clinical information within a shared polygenic architecture.
